Custom Iterable Objects

The container class (like list) should support a function

1. __iter__(callable as iter(container-object)) which returns an object of a
class called an iterator.

2. __next__(callable(    ll bl  as next(iterator_object))(        b     ))

These two functions are interfaces which can be implemented by
traversing through a container

Ex. we may visit only elements in odd position or elements satisfying a
boolean condition – like elements greater than 100

Examples

the list a.

      def __init__(self, mylist):
               self.mylist = mylist
     ddeff __iter__(self):(   lf)

      def __next__ (self):
                  self.i += 1
                    if self.i <= len(self.mylist):

              else:

Based on when the error occurs, errors are classified into two types:

      hybrid interpreter, compiler finds this error.

 try:

•  Handlers only handle exceptions that occur in the corresponding try-block, not

•   Last except clause provide a common and default way of handling all exceptions.

slide_pages.text:
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY (UE26CY151 A,B)

Department of Science and Humanities

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Class 8 content:
Phase, Component, Degrees of freedom, Statement of Gibb’s phase rule, chemical potential

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Free energy in Phase equilibria
All substances have tendency to minimize their Gibbs energy at constant temperature and pressure to attain stable state
At phase equilibrium, the Gibbs free energy of the coexisting phases is the same; therefore, no net phase transformation occurs. 
A system is in stable equilibrium when its Gibbs free energy is at a minimum under the given conditions of temperature and pressure. Phase transformations from one phase to another occur to reduce free energy of the system
Changes in temperature or pressure alter the Gibbs free energy of each phase, which may shift the equilibrium and induce a phase transformation
Gibb’s energy is an extensive property

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Phase 
A phase is defined as any homogeneous and physically distinct part of a system bounded by a surface and is mechanically separable from other parts of the system. It is denoted by P

• Gaseous state : P =1  gases are completely miscible

• Liquid state : P = No. of layers when liquids are immiscible 
                            P = 1 when liquids are completely miscible

• Solid state :  Each solid constitutes a separate phase
                        Each polymorphic form constitutes a separate phase
                           P = 1 for solid solution

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Counting the number of phases
1) Solid ⇌   liquid ⇌   vapour ; P = 3
 Ice in the system is a single phase even if it is present as a number of pieces.

2) Calcium carbonate undergoes thermal decomposition
     CaCO3(s)  ⇌   CaO(s)    +    CO2 (g) 
P= 3; 2 solid phases, CaCO3 and CaO and 
   one gaseous phase, that of CO2

3) Ammonium chloride undergoes thermal decomposition
   NH4Cl(s) ⇌  NH3 (g)   +    HCl (g)
P = 2; one solid, NH4Cl and one gaseous, a mixture of NH3 and HCl

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Components
A component is defined as the smallest number of independently varying chemical constituents using which the composition of each and every phase in the system can be expressed

When no reaction is taking place in a system, the number of components is the same as the number of constituents

While expressing in terms of constituents  zero and negative values are allowed

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Counting the number of components:
1-component system 
e.g.   Pure water ; C = 1
    solid water ⇌  liquid water
2-component system
 Salt hydrate system
e.g. Na2SO4.10H2O ; C=2
Na2SO4.10H2O = Na2SO4 + 10H2O          
Na2SO4.7H2O  = Na2SO4 + 7H2O               
Na2SO4             = Na2SO4 + 0H2O
H2O                   = 0 Na2SO4 + H2O

All the different phases can be expressed in terms of the single constituent water

The composition of all the phases can be expressed in terms of 2 components

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Thermal decomposition of solid CaCO3 in a closed container ; C = 2
        CaCO3 (s) ⇌  CaO(s) + CO2(g)
Though there are 3 species present, the number of components is only two
Phases are :  CaCO3(s), CaO(s) and CO2(g)
Any two of the three constituents may be chosen as the components
If CaO and CO2 are chosen, 
    CaCO3(s) = CaO + CO2
    CaO(s)    = CaO + 0 CO2
      CO2(g)    = 0 CaO + CO2 
If CaCO3 and CO2 are chosen, 
    CaCO3(s) = CaCO3 + 0 CO2
    CaO(s)     = CaCO3  -  CO2
      CO2(g)     = 0 CaCO3 + CO2

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride in a closed system ;C = 1
          NH4Cl (s) ⇌  NH3(g)    +    HCl(g)
Phases are : solid phase of NH4Cl(s)and gaseous phase of NH3(g) and HCl(g)
  solid : NH4Cl (s) = NH4Cl
  gas :    NH3(g) +HCl(g)  = NH4Cl
The composition of both the solid and gaseous phase can be expressed in terms of NH4Cl. Hence the number of components is one; C=1
If additional HCl (or NH3) were added to the system, then C = 2 
The decomposition of NH4Cl would not give the correct composition of the gas phase 
A second component, HCl (or NH3) would be needed to describe the gas phase, therefore C=2

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Degrees of freedom (or variance)

The degrees of freedom or variance of a system is defined as the minimum number of intensive variables such as temperature, pressure, concentration, which must be fixed in order to define the system completely; it is denoted by F
                          OR
The degree of freedom of a system may also be defined as the number of variables, such as temperature, pressure and concentration that can be varied independently without altering the number of phases.
Example : water system
Only 1 phase (solid , liquid or gas)
Both temperature and pressure need to be mentioned in order to define the system; F = 2

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

2 phases in equilibrium, 
 Only one variable, either temperature or pressure need to be specified in order to define the system; F =1
 solid water ⇌  liquid water
 If the pressure on the system is maintained at 1 atm, then the temperature of the system gets automatically fixed at 0oC, the normal melting point of ice

3 phases in equilibrium,
No variable can be changed 
temperature and pressure are fixed, F = 0
solid water ⇌  liquid water ⇌  water vapour
Three phases, ice, water, vapour can coexist in equilibrium at triple point of water at 0.0098oC and 4.58mm of Hg pressure only

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Phase rule
It was given by Williams Gibbs in 1874 

Statement of Gibb’s phase rule
    Provided the equilibrium in a heterogeneous system is not influenced by external forces (gravity, electrical or magnetic forces ) , the number of degrees of freedom (F) of the system is related to number of components (C) and number of phases (P) existing at equilibrium to one another by the equation
                                              F = C – P + 2

Phase equilibria
Phase equilibria between phases exist when chemical potential of a component is equal in all the phases in equilibrium
      e.g. for water at triple point 
                  Solid ⇌  liquid ⇌  vapour
The chemical potential of water will be equal in all the three phases
For systems not at equilibrium, the chemical potential will point to the direction in which the system can move in order to achieve equilibrium viz. , the system moves from higher chemical potential to lower chemical potential

Phase equilibria

When various phases are in equilibrium with one another in a heterogeneous system, there can be no transfer of energy  or mass from one phase to another.
For a system at equilibrium, the various phases must have     the same temperature and pressure and their respective compositions must remain constant all along

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY (UE26CY151 A,B)

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Class 9 content:
Derivation of Gibb’s Phase rule

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Phase equilibria
Phase equilibria between phases exist when chemical potential of a component is equal in all the phases in equilibrium
      e.g. for water at triple point 
                  Solid ⇌  liquid ⇌  vapour
The chemical potential of water will be equal in all the three phases
For systems not at equilibrium, the chemical potential will point to the direction in which the system can move in order to achieve equilibrium viz. , the system moves from higher chemical potential to lower chemical potential

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

When various phases are in equilibrium with one another in a heterogeneous system, there can be no transfer of energy  or mass from one phase to another.
For a system at equilibrium, the various phases must have     the same temperature and pressure and their respective compositions must remain constant all along

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Total number of equations(constraints) :
At equilibrium the chemical potential of particular component is same in every phase in a system
                       µ1α = µ1β = µ1γ  =  ....              (P-1)
                       µ2α = µ2β = µ2γ  =  ....              (P-1)
                       µ3α = µ3β = µ3γ  =  ....              (P-1)
                        


                       µcα = µcβ = µcγ  =  ....              (P-1)
     For C components                               C(P-1)
  Total number of equations or constraints =C(P-1)

  F = Total number of variables – total number of equations
              F =  P(C-1) + 2 – {C(P-1)}
              F=C-P+2
 which is the Gibb’s phase rule

Phase equilibria

Phase diagram
A diagram which represents the conditions under which
a substance exists in different phases in a system

Phase diagram of a 1-component system
F = C- P + 2

Single phase : F = 2 ; Area in a diagram

Two phases in equilibrium : F = 1 ; line in a diagram

Three phases in equilibrium : F = 0 ; point in a diagram

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

High pressure, low temperature: solid phase
High temperature, low pressure : vapour phase
In between : liquid phase

solid     ⇌     liquid
liquid    ⇌    vapour
vapour  ⇌   solid

Phase equilibria

Hybridization and Bonding

Each carbon atom is sp² hybridized.
3 sp² orbitals → 2 C–H σ bonds + 1 C–C σ bond.
1 unhybridized p orbital per C → forms π bond.
Double bond (C=C) = 1 σ bond + 1 π bond.

Molecular Orbital (MO) Description

σ system: strong localized framework bonds.
π system: p-orbitals overlap to form π bonding and π* antibonding orbitals.
HOMO = π orbital, LUMO = π* orbital.
Basis for chemical reactivity of alkenes.

5. Visualize Electronic Structure → Orbital diagrams, density maps, HOMO and LUMO orbitals.

Born - Oppenheimer approximation

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Molecular Spectroscopy

Different types of energies possessed by a molecule

Translational energy (Etrans): by virtue of translatory motion of the molecule
Rotational energy (Erot) : by virtue of rotation of a molecule about its centre of gravity 
Vibrational energy (Evib): by virtue of periodic diaplacement of the atoms of a molecule about its equilibrium position
Electronic energy(Eelec) : due to the different electronic arrangements in the molecule

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Molecular Spectroscopy

Born-Oppenheimer approximation

Total energy of a molecule is the sum of translational, rotational, vibrational and electronic energies, i.e. 
E = Etrans + Erot + Evib + Eelec

Translational energy is negligibly small. Hence Born-Oppenheimer approximation can be written as 
                                              E = Erot + Evib + Eelec

Electronic, vibrational and  rotational energies of a molecule are completely independent of each other 
Because the electronic energy levels are much farther apart than the vibrational energy levels which are again much farther apart than the rotational energy levels
Can be written as 
Erot << Evib << Eelec

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Molecular Spectroscopy

Vibrational Spectroscopy
When a molecule undergoes vibrational changes, it absorbs IR radiation

For a molecule to be vibrationally active (IR active) the vibration of a molecule must be associated with change in dipole moment

 Vibrations of molecules can result in changes in electric dipoles that can interact with the electrical component of the electromagnetic radiation.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Molecular Spectroscopy

When the frequencies match, resonance occurs and the molecule absorbs energy and goes to the higher vibrational levels and exhibits vibrational spectrum

Molecules such as HCl ,CO and H2O will show vibrational spectra while H2, Cl2 will not

CO2 molecule does not possess permanent dipole moment but is IR active as when it vibrates asymmetrically or in bending mode ,there is change in dipole moment

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Molecular Spectroscopy

CO2 molecule although does not possess permanent dipole moment  is IR active because some of its vibrational modes are IR active:
CO2 symmetric stretch is IR inactive as there is no change in dipole moment when molecule vibrates in this mode.
CO2 asymmetric stretch is IR active
CO2 bending mode is IR active

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY (UE26CY151 A,B)

Department of Science and Humanities

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Class 8 content:
Phase, Component, Degrees of freedom, Statement of Gibb’s phase rule, chemical potential

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Free energy in Phase equilibria
All substances have tendency to minimize their Gibbs energy at constant temperature and pressure to attain stable state
At phase equilibrium, the Gibbs free energy of the coexisting phases is the same; therefore, no net phase transformation occurs. 
A system is in stable equilibrium when its Gibbs free energy is at a minimum under the given conditions of temperature and pressure. Phase transformations from one phase to another occur to reduce free energy of the system
Changes in temperature or pressure alter the Gibbs free energy of each phase, which may shift the equilibrium and induce a phase transformation
Gibb’s energy is an extensive property

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Phase 
A phase is defined as any homogeneous and physically distinct part of a system bounded by a surface and is mechanically separable from other parts of the system. It is denoted by P

• Gaseous state : P =1  gases are completely miscible

• Liquid state : P = No. of layers when liquids are immiscible 
                            P = 1 when liquids are completely miscible

• Solid state :  Each solid constitutes a separate phase
                        Each polymorphic form constitutes a separate phase
                           P = 1 for solid solution

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Counting the number of phases
1) Solid ⇌   liquid ⇌   vapour ; P = 3
 Ice in the system is a single phase even if it is present as a number of pieces.

2) Calcium carbonate undergoes thermal decomposition
     CaCO3(s)  ⇌   CaO(s)    +    CO2 (g) 
P= 3; 2 solid phases, CaCO3 and CaO and 
   one gaseous phase, that of CO2

3) Ammonium chloride undergoes thermal decomposition
   NH4Cl(s) ⇌  NH3 (g)   +    HCl (g)
P = 2; one solid, NH4Cl and one gaseous, a mixture of NH3 and HCl

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Components
A component is defined as the smallest number of independently varying chemical constituents using which the composition of each and every phase in the system can be expressed

When no reaction is taking place in a system, the number of components is the same as the number of constituents

While expressing in terms of constituents  zero and negative values are allowed

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Counting the number of components:
1-component system 
e.g.   Pure water ; C = 1
    solid water ⇌  liquid water
2-component system
 Salt hydrate system
e.g. Na2SO4.10H2O ; C=2
Na2SO4.10H2O = Na2SO4 + 10H2O          
Na2SO4.7H2O  = Na2SO4 + 7H2O               
Na2SO4             = Na2SO4 + 0H2O
H2O                   = 0 Na2SO4 + H2O

All the different phases can be expressed in terms of the single constituent water

The composition of all the phases can be expressed in terms of 2 components

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Thermal decomposition of solid CaCO3 in a closed container ; C = 2
        CaCO3 (s) ⇌  CaO(s) + CO2(g)
Though there are 3 species present, the number of components is only two
Phases are :  CaCO3(s), CaO(s) and CO2(g)
Any two of the three constituents may be chosen as the components
If CaO and CO2 are chosen, 
    CaCO3(s) = CaO + CO2
    CaO(s)    = CaO + 0 CO2
      CO2(g)    = 0 CaO + CO2 
If CaCO3 and CO2 are chosen, 
    CaCO3(s) = CaCO3 + 0 CO2
    CaO(s)     = CaCO3  -  CO2
      CO2(g)     = 0 CaCO3 + CO2

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride in a closed system ;C = 1
          NH4Cl (s) ⇌  NH3(g)    +    HCl(g)
Phases are : solid phase of NH4Cl(s)and gaseous phase of NH3(g) and HCl(g)
  solid : NH4Cl (s) = NH4Cl
  gas :    NH3(g) +HCl(g)  = NH4Cl
The composition of both the solid and gaseous phase can be expressed in terms of NH4Cl. Hence the number of components is one; C=1
If additional HCl (or NH3) were added to the system, then C = 2 
The decomposition of NH4Cl would not give the correct composition of the gas phase 
A second component, HCl (or NH3) would be needed to describe the gas phase, therefore C=2

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Degrees of freedom (or variance)

The degrees of freedom or variance of a system is defined as the minimum number of intensive variables such as temperature, pressure, concentration, which must be fixed in order to define the system completely; it is denoted by F
                          OR
The degree of freedom of a system may also be defined as the number of variables, such as temperature, pressure and concentration that can be varied independently without altering the number of phases.
Example : water system
Only 1 phase (solid , liquid or gas)
Both temperature and pressure need to be mentioned in order to define the system; F = 2

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

2 phases in equilibrium, 
 Only one variable, either temperature or pressure need to be specified in order to define the system; F =1
 solid water ⇌  liquid water
 If the pressure on the system is maintained at 1 atm, then the temperature of the system gets automatically fixed at 0oC, the normal melting point of ice

3 phases in equilibrium,
No variable can be changed 
temperature and pressure are fixed, F = 0
solid water ⇌  liquid water ⇌  water vapour
Three phases, ice, water, vapour can coexist in equilibrium at triple point of water at 0.0098oC and 4.58mm of Hg pressure only

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Phase rule
It was given by Williams Gibbs in 1874 

Statement of Gibb’s phase rule
    Provided the equilibrium in a heterogeneous system is not influenced by external forces (gravity, electrical or magnetic forces ) , the number of degrees of freedom (F) of the system is related to number of components (C) and number of phases (P) existing at equilibrium to one another by the equation
                                              F = C – P + 2

Class 9 content:
Derivation of Gibb’s Phase rule

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Phase equilibria
Phase equilibria between phases exist when chemical potential of a component is equal in all the phases in equilibrium
      e.g. for water at triple point 
                  Solid ⇌  liquid ⇌  vapour
The chemical potential of water will be equal in all the three phases
For systems not at equilibrium, the chemical potential will point to the direction in which the system can move in order to achieve equilibrium viz. , the system moves from higher chemical potential to lower chemical potential

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

When various phases are in equilibrium with one another in a heterogeneous system, there can be no transfer of energy  or mass from one phase to another.
For a system at equilibrium, the various phases must have     the same temperature and pressure and their respective compositions must remain constant all along

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Total number of equations(constraints) :
At equilibrium the chemical potential of particular component is same in every phase in a system
                       µ1α = µ1β = µ1γ  =  ....              (P-1)
                       µ2α = µ2β = µ2γ  =  ....              (P-1)
                       µ3α = µ3β = µ3γ  =  ....              (P-1)
                        


                       µcα = µcβ = µcγ  =  ....              (P-1)
     For C components                               C(P-1)
  Total number of equations or constraints =C(P-1)

  F = Total number of variables – total number of equations
              F =  P(C-1) + 2 – {C(P-1)}
              F=C-P+2
 which is the Gibb’s phase rule

.
.
.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Phase diagram
A diagram which represents the conditions under which
a substance exists in different phases in a system

Phase diagram of a 1-component system
F = C- P + 2
For a 1-component system F = 3 – P
Single phase : F = 2 ; Area in a diagram

Two phases in equilibrium : F = 1 ; line in a diagram

Three phases in equilibrium : F = 0 ; point in a diagram

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

High pressure, low temperature: solid phase
High temperature, low pressure : vapour phase
In between : liquid phase

solid     ⇌     liquid
liquid    ⇌    vapour
vapour  ⇌   solid

Solid   ⇌   liquid   ⇌    vapour

Source:http://abyss.uoregon.edu/~js/glossary/triple_point.html

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Application of Gibb’s phase rule F = C-P+ 2 to  1-component system:
Water system
When only 1 phase is present :
C = 1, P = 1; F = 2 ;Temperature and Pressure can be varied independently
Bivariant system

When 2 phases are in equilibrium:
C = 1, P = 2; F = 1  ; Temperature or Pressure can be varied independently
Univariant system

When all 3 phases are in equilibrium:
C = 1, P = 3; F = 0  ;  Neither Temperature nor Pressure can be varied
Invariant system

Represents equilibrium between liquid, vapour and solid water (ice) 
All three phases are present together
F = 0, invariant system
Triple point for water lies at 0.0098 0C and 4.58 mmHg

Critical point “A”:
  the interface between liquid water and water vapour

   a point above which water does not exist in liquid state

   Critical point lies at 3740C and 218 atm pressure

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Metastable equilibrium (OA’):
 Ice fails to form at the triple point and water continues to exist in liquid phase 
 The vapour pressure of the liquid continues along OA’
 This is called super cooled water and represents metastable equilibrium involving liquid and vapour phases.
 Any disturbance will cause the system to go back to stable equlilibrium (OB)
 The vapour pressure of the system in the metastable region is more than that of the stable system ice at the same temperature

Class 10 content:
Reduced phase rule for a 2-component system
Phase diagram of a 2-component Pb-Ag system

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Phase diagram of a  two component system
The phase rule equation is F = C – P + 2
For a 2 component system the ordinary phase rule cannot be used 
 For a two component system, C = 2 then F = 2 – P + 2 = 4 – P
The minimum number of phase is 1; F = 4 – 1 = 3
This requires 3 dimensional space which cannot be explained on the plane of  paper
One of the three variables is kept constant
Measurements in these systems are generally carried out at atmospheric pressure
Pressure may be considered constant ; degrees of freedom is reduced by 1, 
F = C – P + 2 -1

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

The phase rule takes the form F = C – P + 1 and is known as the reduced phase rule
Equilibria such as solid-liquid equilibria are such systems in which the gas phase is absent and hence are hardly affected by small changes in pressure
  Systems in which the gas phase is absent are called condensed systems
 F = C – P + 1 is also known as condensed phase rule

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Phase equilibria

Phase diagram of a 2-component system 

Phase rule for a 2- component system : F = C-P+1
Pressure is constant
Plot is between Temperature and Composition
A and B are miscible in all proportions in the liquid (molten) state

Phase equilibria

Pb – Ag eutectic system

When a mixture of the Pb –Ag is heated till the mixture melts and then cooled:
First crystal of Pb if formed when f.pt. of Pb in the mixture is reached 
On further cooling more solid Pb precipitates and liquid melt becomes richer in Ag
With decrease in temperature more and more solid Pb separates and the liquid melt moves along curve BO
Finally when temperature reaches to that corresponding to point O, solid Ag also starts precipitating
Three phases are present at O: solid Ag, solid Pb and the liquid melt
Further cooling will just result in cooling of solid Ag & Pb

Phase equilibria

Phase diagram of a  two component system
The phase rule equation is F = C – P + 2
For a 2 component system the ordinary phase rule cannot be used

The minimum number of phase is 1; F = 4 – 1 = 3
This requires 3 dimensional space which cannot be explained on the plane of  paper
One of the three variables is kept constant
Measurements in these systems are generally carried out at atmospheric pressure
Pressure may be considered constant ; degrees of freedom is reduced by 1, 
F = C – P + 2 -1

Phase equilibria

The phase rule takes the form F = C – P + 1 and is known as the reduced phase rule
Equilibria such as solid-liquid equilibria are such systems in which the gas phase is absent and hence are hardly affected by small changes in pressure
  Systems in which the gas phase is absent are called condensed systems
 F = C – P + 1 is also known as condensed phase rule

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Computational Chemistry

Introduction
Computational chemistry is a set of techniques  to solve chemistry problems by simulating chemical systems (molecular, biological, materials) to provide reliable, accurate and comprehensive information at an atomic level.

It uses the results of theoretical chemistry incorporated into efficient computer programs to calculate the properties of a molecule.

The first theoretical investigation was done by Walter Heitler and Fritz London in 1927

Scope of computational modeling:
Molecular Properties:
It can be used to accurately predict the physical  and chemical properties of molecules, such as HOMO/LUMO
  and predicting the spectra of UV-Vis, IR and NMR
Reaction mechanism: 
To know the underlying reaction mechanism and the kinetics of a reaction mechanism computational chemistry plays a vital role.
Material design: 
It enables the rational design of new materials with desired properties  such as high electrical conductivity, thermal stability etc.
Drug discovery: 
Computational chemistry plays a pivotal role in design and screening of potential drug candidates by simulating the interactions between the drug molecules and biological targets.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Computational Chemistry

Computational methods:
There are two main methods depending on the starting point theory:

Classical method: | Quantum chemistry method :

These use Newton mechanics to model molecular system.
Atom – Sphere, Bonds – Springs and Electrons are ignored.
Total potential energy of a molecule is given by sum of all the energies of attractive and repulsive forces between atom in structure. | These use quantum mechanics to model the molecular system.
It is based on arrangement of electrons in molecules and interaction of these electrons with electron and nuclei of another molecule.
We consider that electron and all other particle exhibits both particle and wave nature.

Ab initio methods

Molecular mechanics programs use equations based on classical physics to calculate force fields.
It is based on the model of a molecule as a collection of balls ( atoms) held together by springs(bonds).
Its too fast like a very large molecules like steroids can be optimized in seconds and allows geometry optimization .

Semi empirical methods:

Semi empirical calculations are based on Schrödinger equation.

It represents a middle road  between the mostly qualitative results available from molecular mechanics and the high computationally demanding quantitative results from Ab initio methods.

Capable of calculating transition states and excited states.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Computational Chemistry

Ab initio calculations:

Ab initio calculations are based on Schrödinger equation and it describes, among other things, how the electrons in a molecule behave.

The wave function is a mathematical function that can be used to calculate the electrons distribution.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Computational Chemistry

Density functional theory

DFT are like Ab initio and semi empirical calculations, based on Schrödinger equation.

However, unlike the other two methods, DFT does not calculate a conventional wave function, but rather derives the electron distribution directly.

Density functional calculations are usually faster than Ab initio, but slower than semi empirical method.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Computational Chemistry

Advantages of computational chemistry:
Calculations are easy to perform than carrying experiments.
Calculations are less costly, whereas experiments are becoming more expensive
Calculations are safe than performing experiments.

Computational chemistry is not a replacement for experimental studies, but plays an important role in enabling chemists to design and develop the desired chemicals/ products.

lecture_notes.dvi

Ref. Book: Introduction to computational chemistry by Frank Jensen, Wiley publications

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Computational Chemistry

Electronic Structure Determination – Example: Ethylene (C₂H₄)

Ethylene (C₂H₄) is the simplest alkene with a C=C double bond.
Electronic structure explains bonding, reactivity, and spectroscopy.
Combines experimental (spectroscopy) and theoretical (MO theory, computation) approaches.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Computational Chemistry

Hybridization and Bonding

Each carbon atom is sp² hybridized.
3 sp² orbitals → 2 C–H σ bonds + 1 C–C σ bond.
1 unhybridized p orbital per C → forms π bond.
Double bond (C=C) = 1 σ bond + 1 π bond.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Computational Chemistry

Molecular Orbital (MO) Description

σ system: strong localized framework bonds.
π system: p-orbitals overlap to form π bonding and π* antibonding orbitals.
HOMO = π orbital, LUMO = π* orbital.
Basis for chemical reactivity of alkenes.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Computational Chemistry

Computational Determination

Steps:
1. Define geometry of C₂H₄.
2. Select Basis set (Mathematical functions).
3. Apply Method→ orbital energies & density.
4. Solve Equations → Get wave function/Electron Density
5. Visualize Electronic Structure → Orbital diagrams, density maps, HOMO and LUMO orbitals.

Computational Chemistry

Traditional quantum chemical simulations are slow. Each calculation can take hours or even days, depending on the method, molecular size, and computational resources.
Instead of solving wave equations from scratch every time, AI models learn structural patterns from existing quantum datasets.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Computational Chemistry

Scopes
Accelerated molecular discovery: Rapid screening of candidate molecules (for drugs, battery electrolytes, or polymers).
Property prediction: Instantly estimating chemical properties like boiling points, toxicity, or reactivity.
Reaction pathway mapping: Predicting chemical reaction steps, yields, and potential side-products.
Structure generation: Designing new molecules tailored to specific engineering requirements from scratch.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Computational Chemistry

Advantages
Massive speedup: Reduces computation times from hours or days to milliseconds once the AI model is trained.
Scale & Throughput: Broad screening of vast chemical spaces that are computationally impossible with traditional models alone.
Pattern recognition: Uncovers complex, subtle structure-property relationships that humans or traditional formulas might miss.

transcript_segments.text: Hello everyone, welcome back to this course on engineering chemistry. Today we will start with a new module on electrochemical equilibrium.
In this module we are going to study about electrode potential and cell potential. We will derive the Nernst equation. Then we discuss the different types of electrodes.
We will look at reference electrodes and also talk about concentration cells. And finally, we will discuss about ion selective electrodes.
In today's class we will discuss the origin of electrode potential, we will talk about cell potential and we will derive Nernst equation.
Electrochemical equilibria deals with electrochemistry, which is a branch of chemistry which deals with the interconversion of chemical energy and electrical energy.
So we have chemical energy getting converted into electrical energy and vice versa. Now this can be done in two different types of cells galvanic cell and the electrolytic cell.
In the galvanic cell, we have chemical energy getting converted into electrical energy. Now where is this chemical energy coming from? It is the energy in a chemical reaction.

Now the reaction has to be a spontaneous reaction because we are not going to provide any energy from outside. The chemical energy has to produce electrical energy. So the reaction has to be a spontaneous reaction, meaning it should happen on its own.
And since we are going to produce electrical energy, that is power, there has to be exchange of electrons. Therefore, we have to have detox reaction.

So if we are talking of a galvanic cell, we need a spontaneous redox reaction which is going to convert chemical energy to electrical energy. Examples of galvanic cell would be in batteries and fuel cells.
Now another type of cell is the electrolytic cell where the reverse is happening. We convert electrical energy to chemical energy. Electrical energy is provided externally and

We want to get chemical energy, meaning we want to make a chemical reaction happen. So obviously the reaction is not going to be spontaneous. We require a non-spontaneous redox reaction in an electrolytic cell.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Electrochemical equilibria

Origin of Electrode potential
When a metal M is in contact with solution containing its ions Mn+, two reactions are	possible:
Ionisation (Oxidation) 	M ⇌ Mn+ + ne-

Deposition (Reduction) 	Mn+ + ne- ⇌	M

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Electrochemical equilibria

Case I : If ionization is faster than deposition
the metal acquires net negative charge, consequently retards the 	rate  of  ionization  and  increases  the  rate  of  deposition.  This 	ultimately lead to the establishment of equilibrium
the metal electrode gets negatively charged and attracts the layer 	of positive ions at the interface
an electrical double layer is formed at the interface of metal and 	solution known as Helmholtz electrical double layer


M ⇌ Mn+ + ne-

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Electrochemical equilibria

Case II : deposition is faster than ionization
the metal acquires net positive charge, consequently retards the 	rate of deposition and increases rate of ionization. This ultimately 	lead to the establishment of equilibrium.
The metal electrode gets positively charged and attracts the layer 	of negative ions at the interface,
an electrical double layer is formed at the interface of metal and 	solution known as Helmholtz electrical double layer

Mn+ + ne- ⇌	M

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Electrochemical equilibria

Standard electrode potential
	The potential developed at the interface of metal and solution, when the  metal  is  in contact  with  a  solution of  its  own ions  having  unit concentration at 298 K
	In case of gas electrodes the partial pressure of gas is maintained at 1 atmospheric pressure.
It is represented as Eo
Electrochemical Cell
Single electrode potentials cannot be measured hence two electrodes are coupled together to form a cell
Cell notation
e.g. Daniel cell:
Zn(s)/Zn2+ (1M)//Cu2+ (1M) / Cu(s)

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Electrochemical equilibria

Cell potential
The difference in electrode potentials of the electrodes constituting the cell
It is denoted by Ecell
Standard cell potential
Ecell depends on concentration of the ions in the cell, temperature and the partial pressures of any gases involved in the cell reaction.
When all the concentrations are 1M, all partial pressures of gases are 1atm and temperature is 298K, the emf is called Standard cell potential, Eocell
Calculation of Ecell
Ecell = Erhs – Elhs	= Ecathode – E anode
Ecell represents the driving force for the cell reaction to take place
∆ G = - nFECELL
If reaction is spontaneous ∆ G is negative, thus ECELL should be positive
If reaction is non spontaneous ∆ G is positive, thus ECELL should be negative

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Electrochemical equilibria

Electrochemical Series:
In order to predict the electrochemical behavior of an electrode – 	electrolyte system, elements are arranged in the order of their standard 	reduction potentials.
This arrangement is known as electrochemical series.
A negative value indicates oxidation tendency while a positive value
indicates a reduction tendency.

transcript_segments.text: Hello everyone, welcome back to this course on engineering chemistry. We will continue with module six on corrosion chemistry and today we will discuss the types of electrochemical corrosion, that is differential metal corrosion and differential aeration corrosion.
When we say types of corrosion, we have studied that there are two types. One is dry corrosion and the other one is wet corrosion. Dry corrosion, as we understand, is due to

the chemical attack of the environment on the metal surface and it happens in the absence of any conducting medium. But for wet corrosion it has to take place only in conducting medium because what we have

is an electrochemical attack. And since most of the times metals are exposed to conducting medium because there's always moisture in the air, therefore wet corrosion is of more importance to us. So we need to understand what are the different mechanisms

by which this electrochemical attack can take place. So we have different types of corrosion which can happen, that is differential metal corrosion, differential aeration corrosion, piting corrosion and stress corrosion.
Let us understand what is differential metal corrosion. Now, this is also referred to as galvanic corrosion. When we have two

Dissimilar metals in contact with each other and they are exposed to the corrosive environment, that is when we say galvanic corrosion will take place or differential metal corrosion. Now this is a very common situation which we come across where we have two.
Two different metals in contact with each other. Therefore, galvanic corrosion can happen very frequently in metals. Now why does this happen? When we have two different metals

They will have different electrode potentials. The moment they are in contact with each other, one of them which has a greater oxidation tendency becomes the anode, and the one which has lesser oxidation tendency will remain as the cathode.
Now, because there will always be in a change in the electrode potentials, this situation

or formation of anode and cathode can take place very easily. Now because we are we are talking of electrochemical attack, the most important thing which we should see under any situation is how are this anode and cathode getting formed on the surface and in the presence of the
uh medium conducting medium we will have corrosion happening. Now here because one of the metal has a lower electrode potential or rather

Negative electrode potential that becomes the anode, the other automatically becomes a cathode. And we know that it is only the anode which undergoes oxidation and hence gets corroded, whereas the cathode, the metal which has become cathode, will remain unaffected by carrot.

This is what we learned in the previous class when we talked about electrochemical theory of corrosion. Now the driving force for corrosion to happen here is the difference in the electrode potential. More the difference in the electrode potentials of the two metals.

More is going to be the corrosion which will happen, of course, it is only the anode which will corrode. So the difference in the electrode potential will be the driving force for this type of corrosion to take place.
Let us see what will be the reactions. Now the metal part which acted as the anode obviously undergoes oxidation. So M is giving you Mn plus plus N electrons, and at the cathode we have water and

Uh in the presence of oxygen and four electrons giving you four OH minus. Now why did we take these reactions in electrochemical theory of corrosion? We learned that at the cathode there can be different reactions based on the medium. Now we'll consider this most commonly happening because there's always plenty of oxygen.
In the atmosphere, and there is moisture. So, therefore, this is the most common reaction which can happen at the cathode. Now, let us take up some examples. Like we have iron in contact with copper.

Now let us look at what is the electrode potential of iron. It is minus 0.44, and copper is 0.34. So if you look at this situation where we have iron and copper in contact with each other, we will understand from the electrode potentials that
immediately iron is going to become the anode and

Copper will become the cathode. So at the anode we know that there will be corrosion. The metal will get converted into uh its ions, therefore the metal is getting destroyed. Whereas at the cathode we know that copper cannot undergo reduction. So copper remains completely

Unaffected by this type of corrosion when it is in contact with iron. And what will be the reaction which is happening? Just now we said that oxygen with the H2O plus two electron is giving you 2 OH minus. So

Another example, let us take where we have now iron in contact with zinc. Earlier it was iron in contact with copper. Now when you check the electrode potential, standard electrode potential of zinc is minus 0.76, whereas iron is minus 0.44. Therefore, what will happen?
Zinc is a more active metal as compared to iron. Therefore, zinc will now act as the anode and the cathode will now be the iron. So in the case where iron was in contact with copper,
Iron was undergoing corrosion, whereas when it is in contact with zinc, it is zinc which will undergo corrosion. So here zinc is getting

converted to z in two plus plus two electrons and these electrons are moving towards the cathode and at the cathode we have these electrons being taken up with water and oxygen giving you hydroxyl ions. So the product here in this case will be zinc hydroxide whereas

In the first case, where we had iron in contact with copper, we will get copper hydroxide iron hydroxide. Now there could where do we commonly find this kind of corrosion happening? Very common is when we have steel screws or rivets in copper sheets.
Now when we have this copper sheet and we have these steel screws, then that will what will happen we notice that it is the steel screws which are getting
uh corroded whereas the copper remains intact. Now here we have a case where we have a copper uh bolt and iron it or a steel nut. So we have the copper bolt and so bolts and nuts

we see many times that they are made of different metals. Now since we have copper here and this is steel, what will we observe? That it we observe here in this case, in this picture, that it is the steel

uh nut which is getting uh corroded whereas the bolt remains absolutely intact. And similarly if we have a copper sheet with steel screws, there also we will find that the copper sheet remains in sack intact and it's only the
uh the steel screws which will get corroded. And very common again you can see this nice picture which is showing the steel pipe connected to copper plumbing. So

Now we have of course shifted to plastic pipes, but earlier steel pipes used to be used and we have this copper plumbing holding the steel pipe. So we will observe here you see that the edges get completely corroded after some time. But what is getting corroded? It is only the
the steel pipe and not the copper plumbing. So this is a very clear example of galvanic corrosion or differential metal corrosion.

Now let us talk about another type of corrosion that is differential aeration corrosion. Now as the name suggests, now we have the same metal getting exposed to different concentrations of air or oxygen.
Uh this is very commonly seen if you have an iron rod which is lying, you can have a part of it which is exposed to different uh different types of uh uh

concentration of the oxygen could be different in one area and it could be different in the other area. So there will be difference in the concentration of oxygen, and we find that the part of the metal

Which is exposed to lower concentration of oxygen becomes anodic in nature and undergoes corrosion, whereas the other part of the metal which has a higher oxygen concentration becomes cathodic and is unaffected by the
Corrosion. Now, the because of the difference in this oxygen concentration, we are getting something like a oxygen concentration cell on the surface of the metal. And this potential difference will
uh cause the uh current to a small amount of current corrosion current to flow. Let us see what are the reactions and you can see here

Now because the oxygen absorption takes place at the cathole, so higher concentration of oxygen wherever we have.

That area becomes the cathode, whereas the other part where there is less oxygen now becomes the anode, and because it's the anode which undergoes corrosion, that is the metal will take part in this reaction here, whereas here there's a lot of oxygen, so oxygen will be involved.
the is always involved at the cathodic uh region so this area exposed to more oxygen is going to become the cathode whereas the part exposed to less oxygen is going to become the anode.

Now, let us look at some examples of differential aeration corrosion. This is a wonderful example. When you pull out a nail from the wall, what do you observe? The part of the nail which is inside the wall, you can see here the part which was inside the wall.

Sorry, this part which was exposed to less oxygen became the anode and the part exposed to more oxygen now has become the cathode. So we see
We see in this case that the part exposed to

Exposed to less oxygen becomes the anode and the part exposed to more oxygen becomes the cathode. And therefore we see the formation of anode and cathode on the surface of the nail and the part inside the wall which was exposed to less oxygen is getting the same.

getting corroded whereas the part exposed to more oxygen is not getting corroded. Another good example would be a wire mesh. As you can see in the picture, the part where they are crossing each other, the two

outside it is not getting corroded. The reason again the part which is crossing each other there the amount of oxygen is less and therefore that acts as the anode whereas the part exposed to more oxygen now this other part so

These parts you can see are more corroded. You can see the yellowish orangish color over here, the rust getting formed, whereas the other part look intact. That is acting as the cathode. So again, this is a very good example where you can see that the lower oxygen, wherever there is less oxygen,
That part is getting corroded, whereas the part exposed to more oxygen is not getting corroded. And another example would be paper pen inside a paper left for a long time.

What do we see there? The part which is inside the paper has got corroded. All of you would have experienced this. The part which is inside the paper has got corroded, whereas the part which was outside of the paper has not got corroded. Again, this is a very clear

example of differential aeration corrosion the part which was inside the it was exposed to less oxygen and hence acted as the anode and got corroded the part which was outside is exposed to more oxygen and therefore it acted as

So this is about differential aeration corrosion. Now in tomorrow's class, in the next class, we are going to talk about a special type of differential aeration corrosion.

1. Differential metal corrosion  
  Also called galvanic corrosion

  When two dissimilar metals are in contact with each other and are
   exposed to a corrosive environment  

  The two metals differ in their electrode potentials.  The metal with
  lower electrode potential acts as anode and the other metal with
  higher electrode potential acts as cathode 

  The anodic metal undergoes oxidation and gets corroded. The
   cathodic metal remains unaffected

  The driving force for corrosion is the difference in electrode
   potentials of the two metals

  higher electrode potential acts as cathode 

  The anodic metal undergoes oxidation and gets corroded. The
   cathodic metal remains unaffected

  The driving force for corrosion is the difference in electrode
   potentials of the two metals

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

2. Corrosion Inhibitors
  Chemical substances which are added in small quantities to the corrosive environment to decrease the rate of corrosion  
  Inhibitors slow down or inhibit the anodic or cathodic reaction and control corrosion
  They can be used only in confined environment
  The action of an inhibitor depends on the nature of the metal to be protected as well as corrosive environment

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

2 (a) Anodic inhibitors:

                              M → Mn+ + ne- 

If the formation of Mn+ is prevented, the corrosion process is retarded

This is achieved by the addition of large anions such as chromate(CrO42), tungstate (WO42), etc.

These ions combine with Mn+ and form a precipitate which covers the surface of the anode

[Image text, OCR]
Inhibitors coat the surface and prevent corrosion
Metal Surface

Source:http://www.penriteoil.com.au/knowledge-centre/Coolant%20Inhibitor%20Packs/149/what-are-corrosion-inhibitors/289

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

Anodic inhibitors are found to be effective only when sufficient amount of the inhibitor is added into the corrosion medium

If insufficient quantity is added, then a part of the anodic region is exposed to the environment  

Formation of small anodic area results in intense corrosion

Salts like Na2CrO4 , Na2WO4

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

2 (b) Cathodic inhibitors:
 liberation of hydrogen
 absorption of oxygen

Inhibiting any of these reactions will slow down the cathodic reaction which in turn slows down the anodic reaction; corrosion is inhibited

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

Inhibition of hydrogen liberation: 
Preventing the diffusion of H+ ions to the cathode-
 
By the addition of certain organic compounds which contain nitrogen or sulfur

 Aliphatic amines, urea, thiourea, mercaptans, heterocyclic compounds are widely used as cathodic inhibitors

They get adsorbed on the cathodic region forming a protective film, preventing the H+ ions from coming in contact with the cathodic metal surface

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

By increasing the hydrogen overvoltage on the metal
   surface –

  When Hydrogen overvoltage is high , liberation of H2 will be
   difficult

  By the addition of oxides of arsenic, antimony(As2O3, Sb2O3)
   or salts like  sodium meta-arsenite(NaAsO2)

They deposit on the cathode region  

The hydrogen overvoltage on these metals is very high; liberation of H2 is reduced

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

Inhibition of oxygen absorption:

By removing the oxygen from the corrosive media -

By adding Oxygen scavengers like hydrazine

           N2H4 + O2 → N2 + 2H2O

By adding reducing agents sodium sulfite etc.

          2Na2SO3 + O2 → 2Na2SO4

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

By decreasing the diffusion rate of oxygen to cathode – 
By adding salts with large cations such as ZnSO4, MgSO4, NiSO4 etc. 
The cations of the salts (Zn2+, Mg2+) migrate towards the cathode surface and react with the hydroxyl ions formed at the cathode
Zn2+ + 2OH- → Zn(OH)2

Mg2+ + 2OH- → Mg(OH)2
The hydroxides get deposited on the cathodic sites
The protective film impermeable to oxygen prevents its diffusion to the cathodic region

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

Limitations: 

They contaminate the environment

Many of the inhibitors are toxic, cannot be used in systems which come in contact with humans

Can be used only in closed systems in which corrosive environment is either contained or re-circulated

Corrosion Chemistry

3. Impressed current method:

  By applying a direct current

 The protected metal is made cathodic by connecting it to the cathode
   of the external source of current
Anode of the external source is usually connected to an inert electrode
   like graphite; Platinum, silicon, iron are also used as anodes

  A backfill of coke ,bentonite is used to improve efficiency of the anode (The prime purpose of using the backfill is to reduce electrical resistivity. This provides a lower anode-to-earth resistance and greater current outputs in cases where the surrounding soil is of high resistivity).

 The metal structure being cathode does not undergo corrosion

is it is like creating a barrier again it is just creating a barrier between the metal surface and the environment and therefore since the metal is now not exposed to the environment we find that this is going to inhibit the uh anodic reaction and hence control corrosion.

Now this is about the corrosion inhibitors. The anodic inhibitors and the cathodic inhibitors, how they act. So anodic inhibitors we learned that large anions are used like chromate and tungstate.
In the case of cathodic inhibitors, depending on which reaction we are going to stop, if it is liberation of hydrogen, then we use urea, thiourea.

And uh another was to increase the hydrogen over voltage that was also done with the help of arsenic oxide and antimony oxide. So these are examples of corrosion inhibitors, specifically cathodic inhibitors. And there was another set of cathodic inhibitors where you could use oxygen scavengers like

And the last fall, which we have already uh understood, is that they can be used only in closed system. We cannot use them uh in open uh system, but only in closed system in which the corrosion corrosive environment is either

energy

CHEMICAL ENERGY

ELECTRICAL ENERGY

Electrolytic
cell

Galvanic cell

Converts chemical energy to electrical energy

Converts electrical energy to chemical energy

Cells used in
electroplating

Batteries and fuel cells

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Electrochemical equilibria

Electrochemical studies:
Redox reaction
Electrodes- Anode (oxidation)
Cathode (reduction)
Electrolytic conductance through electrolyte due to movement of
ions
Acid, alkali or salt solutions Molten electrolytes
Solid electrolytes
Electrode potential
	When a metal rod is dipped in a solution of its own ions, the electrical potential developed at the interface of the metal and its solution
It is denoted by E

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Electrochemical equilibria

Origin of Electrode potential
When a metal M is in contact with solution containing its ions Mn+, two reactions are	possible:
Ionisation (Oxidation) 	M ⇌ Mn+ + ne-

Deposition (Reduction) 	Mn+ + ne- ⇌	M

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Electrochemical equilibria

Case I : If ionization is faster than deposition
the metal acquires net negative charge, consequently retards the 	rate  of  ionization  and  increases  the  rate  of  deposition.  This 	ultimately lead to the establishment of equilibrium
the metal electrode gets negatively charged and attracts the layer 	of positive ions at the interface
an electrical double layer is formed at the interface of metal and 	solution known as Helmholtz electrical double layer


M ⇌ Mn+ + ne-

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Electrochemical equilibria

Case II : deposition is faster than ionization
the metal acquires net positive charge, consequently retards the 	rate of deposition and increases rate of ionization. This ultimately 	lead to the establishment of equilibrium.
The metal electrode gets positively charged and attracts the layer 	of negative ions at the interface,
an electrical double layer is formed at the interface of metal and 	solution known as Helmholtz electrical double layer

Mn+ + ne- ⇌	M

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Electrochemical equilibria

Standard electrode potential
	The potential developed at the interface of metal and solution, when the  metal  is  in contact  with  a  solution of  its  own ions  having  unit concentration at 298 K
	In case of gas electrodes the partial pressure of gas is maintained at 1 atmospheric pressure.
It is represented as Eo
Electrochemical Cell
Single electrode potentials cannot be measured hence two electrodes are coupled together to form a cell
Cell notation
e.g. Daniel cell:
Zn(s)/Zn2+ (1M)//Cu2+ (1M) / Cu(s)

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Electrochemical equilibria

Cell potential
The difference in electrode potentials of the electrodes constituting the cell
It is denoted by Ecell
Standard cell potential
Ecell depends on concentration of the ions in the cell, temperature and the partial pressures of any gases involved in the cell reaction.
When all the concentrations are 1M, all partial pressures of gases are 1atm and temperature is 298K, the emf is called Standard cell potential, Eocell
Calculation of Ecell
Ecell = Erhs – Elhs	= Ecathode – E anode
Ecell represents the driving force for the cell reaction to take place
∆ G = - nFECELL
If reaction is spontaneous ∆ G is negative, thus ECELL should be positive
If reaction is non spontaneous ∆ G is positive, thus ECELL should be negative

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Electrochemical equilibria

Electrochemical Series:
In order to predict the electrochemical behavior of an electrode – 	electrolyte system, elements are arranged in the order of their standard 	reduction potentials.
This arrangement is known as electrochemical series.
A negative value indicates oxidation tendency while a positive value
indicates a reduction tendency.

A quantitative relationship between electrode potential and concentration of species with which the electrode is reversible

The maximum work that can be obtained is

For an electrochemical system, maximum work done is

Total charge available × Energy available per unit charge

Class 20 content:
Electrochemical Theory of corrosion

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Corrosion Chemistry

Corrosion
	The destruction or deterioration & consequent loss of metal through direct chemical or electrochemical attack by the environment
	Most metals except very noble ones, corrode on contact with water (and moisture in the air), acids, bases, salts, oils, aggressive metal polishes, and other solid and liquid
chemicals
Spontaneous process
Causes indirect losses

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Corrosion Chemistry

Pure metal  undesirable products
Rusting of iron - a reddish brown scale formation on iron
and steel objects
Due to formation of hydrated ferric oxide (Fe2O3.xH2O)
Scaling of Copper - Green scales formed on copper articles
Due to formation of basic cupric carbonate(CuCO3 + Cu(OH)2)

Source:https://opentextbc.ca/che mistry/chapter/17-6-corrosion/

The Statue of Liberty is covered with a copper skin, and was originally brown, as shown in this painting

Exposure to the elements has resulted in the formation of the blue-green patina seen today

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Corrosion Chemistry

Why do metals undergo corrosion?
Most metals occur in nature in the form of their compounds
such as oxides, sulfides, carbonates, chlorides
Metals are extracted from these ores by reduction
which is an endothermic process, energy being supplied in the form of heat or electrical energy
Pure metals are relatively at higher energy state compared to
their corresponding ores, and they have a natural tendency
to revert back to their combined state

Mineral (metal ore)

Corrosion

Extraction

Spontaneous process

Endothermic process

Metal

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Corrosion Chemistry

Types of corrosion
Dry corrosion :
Direct chemical attack due to affinity of the metal to certain gases
In the absence of the electrolytic medium
gases(O2,F2,H2S,NH3)

M

Wet corrosion :
Electrochemical attack on the metal
in the presence of moisture or conducting medium

Conducting medium

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Corrosion Chemistry

Electrochemical theory of corrosion
	A large number of tiny galvanic cells are formed due to the formation of separate anodic and cathodic regions on the metal surface
At the anodic region, metal undergoes oxidation and gets converted into
its ions, liberating electrons and the metal undergoes corrosion
	At the cathodic region, reduction takes place but since the metal cannot be reduced further, metal atoms are unaffected by corrosion

Anode

Cathode

M  Mn+ + ne-

A + ne-  An-

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Corrosion Chemistry

The electrons liberated at the anodic region migrate to the cathodic
region constituting a small corrosion current
The metal ions formed at the anode and some anions formed at the  cathode  diffuse  towards  each  other  through  the  conducting medium andform a corrosion product somewhere between anode and the cathode
Corrosion of metal continues as long as both anodic and cathodic 	reactions	take place simultaneously

1. Differential metal corrosion  
  Also called galvanic corrosion

  When two dissimilar metals are in contact with each other and are
   exposed to a corrosive environment  

  The two metals differ in their electrode potentials.  The metal with
  lower electrode potential acts as anode and the other metal with
  higher electrode potential acts as cathode 

  The anodic metal undergoes oxidation and gets corroded. The
   cathodic metal remains unaffected

  The driving force for corrosion is the difference in electrode
   potentials of the two metals

When a metal is exposed to different concentrations of air (O2), part of the metal exposed to lower concentration of O2 becomes anodic and undergoes corrosion

  When two dissimilar metals are in contact with each other and are
   exposed to a corrosive environment  

  The two metals differ in their electrode potentials.  The metal with
  lower electrode potential acts as anode and the other metal with
  higher electrode potential acts as cathode 

  The anodic metal undergoes oxidation and gets corroded. The
   cathodic metal remains unaffected

  The driving force for corrosion is the difference in electrode
   potentials of the two metals

 Metals with lower electrode potential values are more

2. Nature of the corrosion product: 

For some metals like Chromium, Aluminum etc., the corrosion product formed on the surface of the metal acts as a protective film

 If the corrosion product deposited is insoluble, stable, uniform, and non porous, it acts as a protective film preventing further corrosion of metal

A thin, invisible, impervious, continuous film formed on the surface acts as a barrier between the fresh metal surface and the corrosion environment

Corrosion Chemistry

On the other hand metals like iron, zinc, magnesium, etc., do not form  protective film on the surface of the metal 

 If the corrosion product is soluble, unstable, non uniform, and
  porous, the corrosion continues unabated

  corrosion environment and corrosion of the metal takes place
  continuously

 Steel gets corroded but stainless steel does not

A metal with low hydrogen overvoltage on its surface is more susceptible to corrosion 

Hydrogen evolution is a cathodic reaction

If cathodic reaction is hydrogen evolution type, hydrogen gas is liberated easily and thus the cathodic reaction rate is faster

4. Polarization at anodic and cathodic region: 
Polarisation is the drift in electrode potential of an electrode
Due to change in concentration of species

Anodic polarisation:
At anodic area, metal is oxidized, liberating metal ions which move towards cathodic area
Metal ions liberated at anode cannot move freely towards cathodic area because of opposing factors like lower conductivity of the medium 
Metal ions get concentrated at anodic area and this decreases tendency of metal to undergo oxidation ; corrosion rate falls




Anodic polarisation is due to accumulation of ions in the anodic region

Due to retarded movement of cathodic reactant (O2, H+) towards the cathodic surface or retarded removal of products formed in cathodic region

Hence, the rate of cathodic reaction decreases.  A retarded cathodic reaction results in retardation of anodic reaction also which slows down the corrosion process 

Cathodic polarisation is due to depletion of ions in the cathodic region

Coating of a layer of metal which is anodic to base metal
e.g. , Iron article coated with Zinc

Cathodic metal coating:
Coating of a layer of metal which is cathodic to base metal

Anodic metal coating: 

Coating metal is more active with respect to the base metal

Even if the base metal is not completely covered, it will not undergo pitting corrosion

Galvanizing:
 Coating a layer of zinc on iron is called  galvanization 
The following steps are involved in the process:

Iron sheet is passed through organic solvent or caustic solution to remove oil or grease present on it

 It is washed with dil. H2SO4 to remove any rust, scale or dust present on the surface (pickling)

 It is treated with a mixture of aqueous solution of ZnCl2 and NH4Cl which
  acts as flux which prevents oxidation and then dried

 Finally it is dipped in molten zinc at 425-430o C

 Excess zinc present on iron sheet is removed by passing through hot rollers

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY (UE26CY151 A,B)

Department of Science and Humanities

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

Class 24 content:
Corrosion control
Corrosion inhibitors, Impressed current cathodic Protection, Use of AI tools in corrosion detection and control

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

2. Corrosion Inhibitors
  Chemical substances which are added in small quantities to the corrosive environment to decrease the rate of corrosion  
  Inhibitors slow down or inhibit the anodic or cathodic reaction and control corrosion
  They can be used only in confined environment
  The action of an inhibitor depends on the nature of the metal to be protected as well as corrosive environment

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

2 (a) Anodic inhibitors:

                              M → Mn+ + ne- 

If the formation of Mn+ is prevented, the corrosion process is retarded

This is achieved by the addition of large anions such as chromate(CrO42), tungstate (WO42), etc.

These ions combine with Mn+ and form a precipitate which covers the surface of the anode

[Image text, OCR]
Inhibitors coat the surface and prevent corrosion
Metal Surface

Source:http://www.penriteoil.com.au/knowledge-centre/Coolant%20Inhibitor%20Packs/149/what-are-corrosion-inhibitors/289

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

Anodic inhibitors are found to be effective only when sufficient amount of the inhibitor is added into the corrosion medium

If insufficient quantity is added, then a part of the anodic region is exposed to the environment  

Formation of small anodic area results in intense corrosion

Salts like Na2CrO4 , Na2WO4

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

2 (b) Cathodic inhibitors:
 liberation of hydrogen
 absorption of oxygen

Inhibiting any of these reactions will slow down the cathodic reaction which in turn slows down the anodic reaction; corrosion is inhibited

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

Inhibition of hydrogen liberation: 
Preventing the diffusion of H+ ions to the cathode-
 
By the addition of certain organic compounds which contain nitrogen or sulfur

 Aliphatic amines, urea, thiourea, mercaptans, heterocyclic compounds are widely used as cathodic inhibitors

They get adsorbed on the cathodic region forming a protective film, preventing the H+ ions from coming in contact with the cathodic metal surface

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

By increasing the hydrogen overvoltage on the metal
   surface –

  When Hydrogen overvoltage is high , liberation of H2 will be
   difficult

  By the addition of oxides of arsenic, antimony(As2O3, Sb2O3)
   or salts like  sodium meta-arsenite(NaAsO2)

They deposit on the cathode region  

The hydrogen overvoltage on these metals is very high; liberation of H2 is reduced

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

Inhibition of oxygen absorption:

By removing the oxygen from the corrosive media -

By adding Oxygen scavengers like hydrazine

           N2H4 + O2 → N2 + 2H2O

By adding reducing agents sodium sulfite etc.

          2Na2SO3 + O2 → 2Na2SO4

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

By decreasing the diffusion rate of oxygen to cathode – 
By adding salts with large cations such as ZnSO4, MgSO4, NiSO4 etc. 
The cations of the salts (Zn2+, Mg2+) migrate towards the cathode surface and react with the hydroxyl ions formed at the cathode
Zn2+ + 2OH- → Zn(OH)2

Mg2+ + 2OH- → Mg(OH)2
The hydroxides get deposited on the cathodic sites
The protective film impermeable to oxygen prevents its diffusion to the cathodic region

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

Limitations: 

They contaminate the environment

Many of the inhibitors are toxic, cannot be used in systems which come in contact with humans

Can be used only in closed systems in which corrosive environment is either contained or re-circulated

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

3. Impressed current method:

  By applying a direct current

 The protected metal is made cathodic by connecting it to the cathode
   of the external source of current
Anode of the external source is usually connected to an inert electrode
   like graphite; Platinum, silicon, iron are also used as anodes

  A backfill of coke ,bentonite is used to improve efficiency of the anode (The prime purpose of using the backfill is to reduce electrical resistivity. This provides a lower anode-to-earth resistance and greater current outputs in cases where the surrounding soil is of high resistivity).

 The metal structure being cathode does not undergo corrosion

  Anode being inert remains unaffected

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

Advantages:
One installation can protect large area of metal

Limitations:
Rather expensive, since it needs high current for safe protection of structure

If the impressed current is not uniform on the entire surface of the protected structure, localized corrosion takes place on the protected metal

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

If hydrogen liberation is the cathodic reaction on the metal surface, then the protected metal may suffer from hydrogen embrittlement

Hydrogen embrittlement:
H2 molecule being small enters the metal lattice and when the pressure increases , it causes blisters and makes the metal brittle

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY

AI in Corrosion Detection and Control- Introduction 
Conventional inspection methods are often periodic, labor-intensive, and may fail to detect corrosion at an early stage.

By integrating AI with smart sensors, coating monitoring systems, drones, and robotic inspections, industries can detect corrosion before severe damage occurs and implement timely protective measures.

[Image text, OCR]
vidya
38645

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

AI Assisted proactive infrastructural corrosion management Process

Capture images/Inspection Data: Images, sensor measurements, and electrochemical readings are collected from the assets. 
AI Model: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and other machine learning algorithms analyze the inspection data to identify corrosion patterns. 
Detection & Severity Assessment: The AI model detects corrosion, identifies its type, and assesses its severity and extent. 
Corrosion Rate & Remaining Life Prediction: The AI model predicts the corrosion progression rate and estimates the remaining service life of the asset. 
Control Actions: Based on the AI predictions, appropriate maintenance strategies, protective coatings, cathodic protection, and repair actions are recommended to mitigate corrosion.

STEP 1&2 : Capture Images and Data input 
Inspection Data
Capture Images/Collect Sensor Data(Images, Sensors and EIS)

4. Identification
Detection and severity
(type of Corrosion)

5. Forecasting
Rate and Life prediction
(RUL and Corrosion rate)

6. Decision and Action
(Maintenance and protection Planning)
 Predictive maintenance, Coating monitoring, Smart sensors, Drones & robots

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Corrosion Chemistry

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is thus transforming corrosion management by enabling continuous monitoring, early defect detection, predictive maintenance, and intelligent decision-making.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY (UE26CY151 A,B)

Department of Science and Humanities

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Experiential Learning – UNIT 2 (supplementary material)

Temperature: 
 The rate of a chemical reaction, in general, increases with rise in temperature

 For corrosion process (redox reaction) , the rate of corrosion increases
  as the temperature increases as
 Increase in rate of reaction
Increase in conductance of the medium- ions migrate fast at higher temperature.
Decrease in the polarization effects at the anodic and cathodic sites
Increase in solubility of corrosion product in the medium
Breakdown in the protective film that might exist on the surface

 However, if corrosion is due to dissolved gases like O2, CO2, etc., the rate of corrosion decreases with increase in temperature as the solubility of these gases in the medium decreases

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Experiential Learning – UNIT 2 (supplementary material)

pH: 
  In general, lower the pH of the corrosion medium, higher is the
    corrosion rate
At low pH ,concentration of H+ ions is high; H+ ions help for cathodic reaction facilitating anodic oxidation of the metal
2H+ + 2e- → H2
Corrosion product becomes more soluble in acidic 
  medium
        However, some metals like Al undergo fast corrosion in
        highly alkaline solution as their corrosion product is
        soluble in alkaline medium

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Experiential Learning – UNIT 2 (supplementary material)

Electrical conductivity of the corrosion medium: 

As the conductivity of the corrosion medium increases, the corrosion rate also increases

Higher the conductivity of the medium, faster the ions can migrate between the anodic and cathodic regions of the corrosion cell

Faster will be the exchange of electrons at the electrode surfaces; corrosion rate increases

 Corrosion is more in saline water

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Experiential Learning – UNIT 2 (supplementary material)

Humidity: 
Corrosion rate increases with increase in the humidity in the medium. 
The presence of moisture in the atmosphere provides the conducting medium for the formation of galvanic cell, facilitating corrosion of the metal.

Reserve  batteries

One of the key component is kept separated from the rest of the battery and
 Is allowed to come in contact with other components when required
 Usually the electrolyte is the component that is isolated

Working of Glucose Biosensor
Developed by Updike and Hicks 
Enzyme Glucose oxidase(GOx) catalyze the oxidation of glucose by molecular oxygen producing glucolactone and hydrogen peroxide.
In order to work as a catalyst, GOx requires a redox cofactor –flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), works as an initial electron acceptor and is reduced to FADH2. 
Glucose + GOx –FAD   Glucolactone + GOx – FADH2

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Sensors

Working of Glucose Biosensor

The cofactor is regenerated by reacting with oxygen, leading to the formation of hydrogen peroxide 
GOx – FADH2 + O2   GOx – FAD + H2O2 
 Hydrogen peroxide is oxidized at a platinum electrode. 
The number of electron transfers, at electrode surface is directly proportional to the number of glucose molecules present in the blood. 
H2O2  2H+ +O2 + 2e-

Batteries: Components, working & classification

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Battery 
Device which stores chemical energy and converts it into electrical energy on demand

Alternate sources of energy
Variable sizes and shapes
Portable

Applications : Consumer goods - mobiles, laptops , 
    calculators, flash lights	             
    emergency lighting,  space vehicles, electric vehicles, 
    pacemakers

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Components of a battery
 Anode :  Oxidation takes place
                     Electroactive material : metals which can undergo oxidation easily  
                     Zn, Pb, Li
 Cathode :  Reduction takes place
                    Electroactive material : compounds which can undergo reduction easily
                     PbO2, MnO2, O2 
 Electrolyte: Substance with good ionic conductivity
                      Acid, alkali or salt solutions; solids- doped oxides, polymers
                        H2SO4, KOH, Nafion
 Separator: Insulator which separates anode and cathode compartment    
                       Role -  To prevent internal short circuit 
                       Transport ions from anode to cathode compartments and vice versa 
                       Polypropylene, Cellophane

Based on working, two types of batteries:
Primary battery
Electroactive material cannot be regenerated
Discarded after electroactive species is consumed
Galvanic cell
Dry cell, Li-MnO2

Secondary battery
Electroactive material can be regenerated
Can be used several times
Galvanic as well as electrolytic cell
Storage battery
Li-ion, Pb-acid, Ni-Cd

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Reserve  batteries

One of the key component is kept separated from the rest of the battery and
 Is allowed to come in contact with other components when required
 Usually the electrolyte is the component that is isolated
  This prevents chemical reaction between the cell components (self discharge)
   Has unlimited shelf life
   Usually designed for emergency use e.g mid-air crisis
Examples: Mg-AgCl(water activated) , Zn-Ag2O(KOH activated)
Applications: Sonobuoys, Weather balloons, Emergency lights etc.,

Electricity Storage density: 
 Amount of charge or electricity per unit weight which the battery can hold
            ESD= Capacity/ Weight of the battery
Weight includes weight of all the components of the battery - electrodes, electrolyte, case, current collectors, terminals etc 
To get high  electricity storage density, use of right kind of material for all the components is important
e.g.,  7g of Li is required at anode to give 1F of charge whereas 104g of Pb is required for the same amount of charge

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Cycle life : 
 Number of charge/discharge cycles that are possible before failure occurs
 Applicable only to secondary batteries

 Reasons for limited cycle life: 
 Corrosion at contact points 

 Shedding of active material from the plates

 Shorting between electrodes due to irregular crystal 
  growth and changes in morphology
