ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Modern batteries

Zinc air batteries

Metal-air battery
 Anode : Zn ; Cathode : O2 
 Alkaline battery ; electrolyte : alkali
 Uses oxygen directly from the atmosphere to produce 
  electrochemical energy
 Cathode active material need not be stored inside the  
  battery
 Energy density is very high

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Construction:
Anode : Zinc granules with gelling agent ( to immobilize the composite and ensure adequate contact with Zinc granules) and a small amount of electrolyte
Cathode: Carbon (graphite) blended with MnO2(catalyst) with a wet proofing agent coated on nickel wire mesh support and an outer layer of air permeable Teflon layer. Air access holes on the cathode provide pathway for O2 to enter the battery
Electrolyte : 30% KOH
Separator : Polypropylene membrane soaked in electrolyte

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Advantages : 
High energy density : Air is taken directly from atmosphere and need not be stored ; doesn't contribute to the mass of the battery
      Very long shelf life : It can be kept sealed
     Can be miniaturized 
      No ecological problems
      Low cost
Disadvantages : 
        Limited power output
 Along with air, CO2 may enter the battery.  It reacts with 
        KOH to from K2CO3 , which will reduce the efficiency
                         CO2 + 2KOH  K2CO3  + H2O

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Applications : 
As power source in hearing aids
In various medical devices
In voice transmitters
      Large zinc-air batteries are used in rail-road signaling

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Lithium  batteries

Lithium is a popular anodic material:
Light weight metal. The electrochemical equivalence of lithium is high (7g of lithium can give 1F of charge)
High negative standard reduction potential of -3.05V ; when  coupled with other electrodes gives high voltage
        ( about 4V)
Aqueous electrolytes cannot be used as Lithium is  very reactive and it reacts vigorously with water . So organic and inorganic electrolytes are used

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Components of Lithium batteries: Lithium is used as anode; Cathode can be MnO2, SO2Cl2. Electrolyte can be Li salt in organic solvents like acetonitrile, propylene carbonate or inorganic solvents like SOCl2 
Types of Lithium batteries : 
Primary batteries which are not rechargeable, e.g.  Li-MnO2 
Secondary batteries which are rechargeable, e.g. Solid state lithium metal battery

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Advantages of lithium batteries
 High Voltage up to 4V
 High energy density – Lightest metal
 High tolerance to service conditions  (-40 oC to 70 oC) 
 High electricity storage density
 Flat discharge characteristics

Disadvantages of lithium batteries
 Safety concerns due to high reactivity of Lithium metal 
 Poor cycle life – due to dendrite formation
 Transportation limit

Disadvantages of lithium batteries
 Safety concerns due to high reactivity of Lithium metal

Class 31 content: 
Fuel Cells: Principle, working & H2-O2 fuel cell

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Fuel cells

Chemical energy   Thermal energy  Mechanical energy  Electrical energy 	
                                                Fuel cell
Galvanic cell which converts chemical energy of a fuel oxidant system directly into electrical energy by means of redox reactions
Do not store energy but convert chemical energy in the fuel to electrical energy
Fuel and oxidising agents have to be continuously supplied at the respective electrodes
Generate power as long as the electroactive material is supplied

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Working:

Anode : Fuel   Oxidation product + ne-
Cathode : Oxidant + ne-   Reduction products



Fuels : H2, CO, CH3OH, C2H5OH, HCHO, N2H4
Oxidants: O2 , H2O2, halogens

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Advantages :
 High power efficiency (about 50 - 80% )
 Ecofriendly -  products formed are not toxic
 Silent operation
Disadvantages : 
 Cost of the power is high as a result of the use of  
        expensive electrodes and catalysts
 Power out put is moderate
 Fuels in the form of gases and oxygen need to be stored in
        tanks under high pressure-special equipment is required

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Applications:

  Space exploration; as auxiliary power generators in space
       vehicles
   Vehicle traction for cars, buses and commercial vehicles
   Large scale power generation

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Alkaline fuel cell - H2 – O2 alkaline fuel cell
  Aqueous solution of KOH is used as electrolyte
  Low temperature fuel cell (operates at 100oC) 
  Oxygen reduction is more rapid in alkaline electrolytes 
         than in acid electrolytes
  Use of non noble metal electro-catalyst is feasible
  Carbon containing fuels cannot be used as CO2 is
        formed as product which reacts with the electrolyte, KOH, to form K2CO3 which reduces efficiency of the cell
                  CO2 + KOH  K2CO3 + H2O

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Energy Storage Devices

Construction : 

Anode : Porous carbon with Pt catalyst
Cathode : Porous carbon with Ag catalyst
Fuel : Hydrogen gas      
 Oxidant : Oxygen gas
Electrolyte : 30-45 % KOH(warm)

Energy Storage Devices

H2 gas diffuses through anode ,gets adsorbed on the electrode surface ,reacts with OH- to form water
 At cathode O2 diffuses through electrode, is adsorbed and reduced to OH-
 Product is water which dilutes the KOH

The water was used by astronauts for drinking on Apollo spacecraft

 Emf = 1.23 V

Operates at low temperature
Alkali is used as electrolyte hence non noble metal catalyst  can
        be used so less expensive

Disadvantages:

Reactants must be free from C, because on oxidation CO2 is formed .The alkali reacts with CO2 to form carbonates which reduce efficiency of the cells; pure fuel and oxidant which are free of carbon compounds must be used
Liquid electrolytes pose handling problems

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY

Direct CH3OH-O2 Polymer electrolyte  membrane fuel cells

Known as proton exchange membrane fuel cells
 Polymer membrane or proton exchange membrane is used as electrolyte
 Ease of transport and storage of methanol, an energy-dense yet 
   reasonably stable liquid at all environmental conditions
 Low temperature fuel cell ( 60- 90 °C )
 Low weight and volume
 High energy density
 Noble metal catalyst usually Pt
 CO, if present poisons the catalyst , so pure fuel and oxidant should be
  used

Energy Storage Devices

Construction:
 Anode: Porous carbon electrode containing platinum   
 Cathode : Porous carbon electrode containing platinum 
 Fuel:  Solution of CH3OH     
 Oxidant: Oxygen gas
 Electrolyte: proton conducting polymer membrane
 Membrane should be  an electronic insulator but an excellent conductor of H+ ions

Energy Storage Devices

Electrolyte :
 Fluorocarbon backbone (-CF2-CF2-) similar to Teflon to which sulphonic   acid groups(-SO3H) are attached

The protons on sulphonic acid group are free to migrate through the    hydrated membrane

Water management is very important for Proton exchange membrane fuel cells
Temperature has to be maintained constant (60-90oC)
 Polymer membrane must remain hydrated to maintain H+ conductivity
Water produced from the reaction must be removed from the cathode

 High temperatures

 the polymer may degrade and crack resulting in short circuit

 Low temperatures 
 will result in flooding of the cell thereby reducing efficiency of
  the cell
 a higher catalyst loading will be required

Energy Storage Devices

Advantages: 
 High energy density - due to the low weight of the polymer 
 Long life -  Low temperature operation allows them to start quickly  and
   results in less wear on system components, resulting in better durability
 No free corrosive liquid in the cell

Disadvantages: 
Noble metal catalysts have to be used (Pt) and electrolyte is expensive so  cell cost is high
 CO , if present, poisons the Pt catalyst , hence pure reactants should be used
 Management of carbon dioxide created at the anode  and water management pose 
  problems

 a higher catalyst loading will be required

     • Hydrogen is produced from coal by gasification process

    • Processes use light energy to split water into hydrogen

    • One of the potential for sustainable hydrogen

    • Low environmental impact
    • Yet in early stage of research
 •Electrolysis
    • uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen
    • Electrolysis reaction takes place in a unit called an

    • Method is promising option for carbon-free hydrogen
      production from renewable and nuclear resources.

   2.Acid Electrolysis

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Hydrogen energy

 Alkaline Electrolysis

 Construction

 •Anodic materials: Ni and its alloys
 •Cathodic materials: Cu, Pt
 • Electrolyte : KOH, NaOH (20-40 wt %)
 •Catalyst: Ni-Co-Au, RuO2
 •Operation temperatures are between 343 – 363 K
 •Operating pressure up to 3 Mpa





                                                                                                                  9

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Hydrogen energy
 Working Principle:
  • Pure water is the very poor conductor of electricity
   because splitting of water is very less, hence acid
    (H2SO4 in acid electrolyzer) or base (KOH or NaOH in
    Alkaline  electrolyzer)   is  used  to  improve  the
    conductivity
  Reactions:
    • Anode: 2OH-  ½ O2 + H2O + 2 e-
    • Cathode: 2H2O + 2e-  H2 + 2OH-
  • Overall Reaction:
   2H2O (liquid)  + Energy  2H2(gas) + O2 (gas)

 Hydrogen energy
Photocatalysis





   This reaction is thermodynamically uphill it does
   not happen on its own. It requires a minimum of
  ΔG° = +237 kJ/mol of Gibbs free energy, which
   translates to a minimum potential of 1.23 V per                                   11
   electron transferred

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Hydrogen energy
Mechanism of Water Splitting

    • Photon absorption: TiO2 absorbs a photon (hν ≥ Eg).

    • Charge generation: Electrons get excited from VB to
      CB, leaving holes in the VB.

    • Separation & migration: Charge carriers (electrons and
        holes) migrates to the surface of the photocatalyst.

     • Surface redox: H⁺ reduced to H2; water oxidised to O2.


      Oxidation in valance band  : 2 H2O + 4 h⁺ → O2 + 4                https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10                                                                                   .1080/01614940.2024.2446476
      H⁺
      Reduction in conduction band : 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ → 2 H2
        Overall reaction   : 2 H2O → 2 H2 + O2



                                                                                                                  12

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Hydrogen energy

 Factors Affecting Efficiency:

 •Band gap of the photocatalyst
 •Light intensity and wavelength
 •Electron-hole recombination
 •Surface area of the catalyst
 •Use of cocatalysts (Pt, Ni, MoS₂)
 •pH of the reaction medium

Role of oxygen sensor in automobiles 
Principle : 

Stoichiometric air/fuel ratio ideal for combustion of gasoline is 14.7:1  

Located in the exhaust stream and indirectly determine air to fuel ratio

O2 sensor allows engine control system to maintain ideal ratio across various engine operating systems

It compares the amount of O2 in the exhaust to the amount of O2 in the atmosphere

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Sensors

An output voltage is generated based on the difference in O2 concentration in the exhaust and atmosphere

An output voltage of 0.2V represents a lean mixture and 0.8V represents a rich mixture
Ideal set point is around 0.45 V

The voltage is sent as feedback to Engine control unit which adjusts the air/fuel ratio back to stoichiometric value 

    Lean mixture results in more of NOX emissions
    Rich mixture leads to more of CO , C particles and unburnt
      fuel emissions

Based on solid state electrochemical fuel cell

Operates at a minimum temperature of 360oC

Stoichiometric air/fuel ratio ideal for combustion of gasoline is 14.7:1

NH group here and CO here, the next one cannot be NH and CO, it has to be CO and NH because it is formed from the diamine, so NH and NH and then again we have CO that is the amide linkage here. Now this will be this molecule is will have will be

that the hydrogen and the oxygen the hydrogen of the amine and the oxygen of the CO are coming very close, they are very in close proximity and that would result in formation of hydrogen bond. So there are so many hydrogen bonds

know that in nylon 66 also we have similar amide linkages but nylon is not as strong as Keblard what could be the reason for that the reason is that in nylon between the uh the amide linkages there is an allephatic chain

C6. Now that C6 has been replaced by an aromatic ring here. Now because of this aromatic ring, this is giving a lot of firmness to Kepler. If it's an elephatic chain, we know it will be more flexible. Whereas now it is in the form of an aromatic ring.

And another reason for this is aromatic stacking. Now we can see here that the benzene rings are lying one above the other. So you can see here if this kind of arrangement happens, then there is a weak interaction between these

To the polymer, and therefore we find that keevlar is very strong. So, why is Kevlar five times stronger than steel on an equal weight basis? The answer is there are two reasons. One is the extensive hydrogen bonding.
between chains of kevlar and additional strength is coming from aromatic stacking.

now have many more applications. So what is the use of making a composite like this? This matrix matrix when you have and these fibers are embedded in it, then any force which is applied onto the

transcript_segments.text: Hello everyone, welcome back to this course on engineering chemistry. We will continue with module seven on functional materials, that is, polymers.

Today we will talk about another polymer composite that is carbon fiber. We talk about the synthesis, properties and applications and finally we will look at the composite of carbon fiber which is known as carbon fiber reinforced polymer.
What are carbon fibers? Basically, they are fibers which are made mostly of carbon atoms, and the diameter is just about 5 to 10 micrometers.
When you compare this diameter with the human hair, as you can see in the picture here, the human hair is much much thicker as compared to the carbon fiber.
So they are very very thin fibers and several thousands of these fibers are twisted together to make a yarn and from that yarn the fabric is woven.
So how do we synthesize this carbon fiber? Now each carbon filament is produced from what we call as a precursor polymer like polyacrylonitrile or pitch, etc.
Now let us study how we are going to prepare this carbon fibre from polyacrylo nitrite.
So initially polyacrylonitrile is made by polymerization of acrylonitrile. So we studied in the uh when we were talking about addition polymerization that
in the in case of ethylene, if we take ethylene and we substitute with a cyanide group, what we get

On polymerization is known as polyacrylonitrile. So simple polymerization will happen and we will get polyacrylonitride. So now the next step, how we are going to use this polyacrylonitrile to uh get the carbon fiber.

Now one thing we have to remember that the carbon fiber has a graphite like structure. So when we are talking about synthesis, we have to keep in mind how to arrive at that graphite like structure. So here again the first step would be polymerization which I mentioned just now.

So we have this acrylonitri which have which has been polymerized and that gives you polyacrylonitrile. Now you can see here of course these acrylonitrile are placed in such a way that they will polymerize
So you have to place them like this. So all these acrylonitrile molecules are going to be placed like this because it is renal cyanide. So this is how these

phil uh acrylonitrile monomers are placed and then polymerization is initiated. So when polymerization happens what is going to happen? The polymerization will always take across take place across the double bond. So this double bond is now going to

uh open up and then we get a polymer which is getting formed it says double bond is gone now and we get cyclic uh the polymerization which happens like this and that's what you can see here in this picture. So you can see the uh
chain has got formed because of the opening of this double bond. Okay. So that is the first step which is

Polymerization. Now the next step is we need to cyclize it. Remember that we want a graphite like structure. So the next step would be cyclization that is done at a low temperature. Now here again we have these cyanide C triple bond N. So what is going to happen during this cyclone?

Cyclization process there will be a bond which will be formed between this carbon and this nitrogen. So basically, once here, if you see the polymerization after it happens, this chain has got formed, and now between this nitrogen, there's a triple bond. So one of the bonds is going to open.

Up and you get a bond getting formed between C and N, and here it will be left with double bond. That's exactly what you can see in this picture, and that will result in a cyclic kind of molecules, and therefore that is called as the cyclization process. So the whole

Polymer now has become cyclic is constituted of cyclic chains, or you can see here cyclic rings, and these are in the form of a chain. So this is the second step that is cyclization at low temperature. So now the next step would be
I want a double bond here. Now that

Because we want to go towards a graphite like structure. I want a double bond here. How do I get it? That is done by the oxidative treatment. So cyclization is the second step which we saw here. This is the cyclization, and the third step would be oxidative treatment, which is done at a higher temperature.

Now this was at low temperature. This is done at a higher temperature. Now what would happen due to oxidation? Obviously, it is treated with oxygen and water molecule will be eliminated, and here basically we are removing hydrogen. This
Hydrogen that is unsaturation now came up. So obviously hydrogen has been removed, and of course we are doing it. Uh we are basically causing oxidation of this um.
uh this small uh this chain polymer over here. So what we get is an unsaturation at these positions. So now the next step is the most important step where we are going to go towards the graphite like

structure. Now but before that if you do uh at a slightly lower temperature we find that these ribbons they are formed like ribbons now two three ribbons like so many of them one place one below the other they start joining together and of course again hydrogen is getting eliminated. So you're coming closer to

graphite like structure now what is missing here it is that there are still some nitrogen atoms present here so as you go on increasing the temperature give it a treatment at a higher temperature then we find that more of these will now if you have three like this now another three will join together

and you get start getting the carbon fiber with the elimination of this nitrogen. Of course the last step would be where you remove all other elements except carbon because we want a graphite like structure that is made of carbon.

So graffiti is the final process and that is done at a very high temperature and in an inert atmosphere and inert atmosphere because you're treating it taking the fibre to such a high temperature, so it will it'll become uh inflammable, it may catch fire. So we have to do it in a
inert atmosphere. So by this process starting from acrylonitrile you got polyacrylonitrile then you cause the cyclization of this chain polymer and then we call we made it

We got some unsaturation in these positions by oxidative treatment and finally we heated it and we got the ribbon like structures joined together to give you this type of structure and finally when it is graffitized, that's called graphitization at a very high temperature.
Then we get what we call as the carbon fiber.

Now this is the process by which we can get the carbon fiber. So what do we understand that this carbon fiber has to have a graphite like structure. Now what is a graphite like structure? If you remember graphite is made up of it, it has a layer structure and

These chains between these layers actually there is a uh uh there is just Vanderwall force of attraction. So so these chains actually slip. But we do that carbon fiber is one of the strongest uh uh material.

So how is that possible? Now the structure if you see these uh consists of sheets of carbon just like we have in graphite, but they are not arranged in a regular pattern. In graphite we have very regular pattern these

lay of carbon they are just one below the other and because they're all sp2 hybridized so we have layers like this and these chains between the chains is just one wall force and the these chains can slip against each other. So your carbon fiber is also a graphite like structure as you can see. But
It is known as a turbostratic arrangement. What is that? These sheets of carbon fiber are half as a leaf folded or crumpled together. So now what happens? They are all
folded and crumpled so as a result that slipping of chains is not possible and this is known as the turbostratic arrangement and that gives the carbon fiber uh a good strength.

Now uh properties we can understand yes, it has very high strength to weight ratio, it is very corrosion resistant and very chemically stable, it has good tensile strength, it is non-poisonous and biologically inert. So basically we are seeing

Say that it is also biocompatible. It is a fiber which is biocompatible and it has a low coefficient of thermal expansion. So it has wonderful properties. Of course, the most used property is high strength to weight ratio.

What would be the applications? It's very clear such a strong material we have. It is used in aerospace, road and marine transport, it is used in sporting goods and medical applications in prostesis surgery. Now this is and also in implants tendon.
Ligamentary repair of those.

Why? Because it is biocompatible. So carbon fibers can be used for uh for skin grafting, etc. Then we also have automobile goods, novel tooling, casings and bases for electronic equipment, EMI and RF shielding brushes.
So audio equipment, loudspeakers or hi-fi equipment, pickup arms, robo arms, wherever uh you need the polymer to be very strong, uh we are going to use this carbon fiber.

But what we have learnt now is about the advantages. Now just let us look at the disadvantages. Of course, it is very expensive due to the large ex energy expenditure. So producing a carbon fibre itself is very expensive, and that's why we don't

find too many consumer goods which are using this carbon fiber, but it is understood that as the manufacturing becomes more and more and the use of carbon fiber becomes more and more then it is the price is definitely going to uh come down and we will have lot of consumer goods

Which are going to use carbon fiber, especially where a lot of strength is required. And one more disadvantage would be volatile byproducts are formed. Like for example, H Cn could be formed when we are making carbon fiber from polyacrylonitrile. So these are the disadvantages.

So, what we have talked about now is just the carbon fiber, which has such wonderful properties. So, if we want to make a composite out of it, then we can understand that this is going to further make the material very, very strong.

So, how will we make this composite? We know that when we make a composite, there has to be a fiber that is the carbon fiber, and the matrix is the epoxy resin. So we are going to combine the two, they will be cured at high temperature and pressure, and we are going to get what we call a
the carbon fiber reinforced polymer so once again it is the metrics like this and we have these fibers embedded in here so depending on what exactly you want to prepare so these embedded fibers

uh are into the matrix. So if we need high impact strength or any lot lot of force is applied on this material, the matrix is going to take the impact of that uh force and it will get dissipated. So therefore
That is how it is getting the strength. Now, what would be the properties? Of course, we know light weight and high strength to weight ratio, low coefficient of thermal expansion.
But one new property which has come here and very very important is the high electrical conductivity. Why? Because we know it has a graphite like structure and we know that graphite.
is conducting in nature. So because of that we find that it has high electrical conductivity. So what would be the applications of such a polymer composite

we know that there are going to be a number of application like in all fields, in various fields, like say sports equipment, then energy production, then consumer goods or power uh portable uh power sources then coastics

because the fibers can be used over there and uh so on like there are so many and then uh of course in aerospace industry then for automobile civil engineering so all these areas we find a lot of application for this
the polymer composite of carbon fibre. So in the next class now we are going to talk about a new class of polymers which are called conducting

Polymers so far polymers were always thought of as insulators, but yes, there is a class of polymers which are which can actually conduct as good as that of the metal, and these are known as conducting polymers. Thank you.

They use organic molecules and hence the name organic light emitting diodes. The phenomena which is happening in OLEDs is called electroluminescence. Therefore, OLEDs
have an emissive electroluminescent layer, which is a film of an organic compound that emits light in response to an electric current. Hence they are also known as organic electroluminescent diodes.

and light is emitted. One example of a polymer which is used. So we should understand that it could be organic molecules or polymers which can make up these conductive layer, this conductive layer and the emissive layer. So in emissive layer we use polyflorine

transcript_segments.text: Hello everyone, welcome back to this course on engineering chemistry.

Today we will look at module eight and that is about green chemistry and this is the only class in this module. So we are going to discuss about green chemistry. We will study the definition and the twelve principles of green chemistry.
Green chemistry is defined as the utilization of a set of principles that reduces or eliminates the use of

use or generation of hazardous substances in the design, manufacture, and application of products. So how is it different from environmental chemistry? We all are aware of environmental chemistry where we talk about removing eliminating
pollution removing pollution from the environment. But here green chemistry talks about
Removing pollution, yes, but not generating it in the first place itself. So it's a concept where we talk of reducing or eliminating the use

of hazardous substances and even generation of hazardous substances where is starting from the design to the manufacture and application of products. So this was definition was coined by Paul T. Anistos and John C. Warner. So what are
The what is the focus of green chemistry? So green chemistry talks about reduction, recycling, and or eliminating toxic substances. Then

we have to find creative alternative routes to minimize impact on the environment. So it is basically a concept and when we have the principle, we keep it in mind and we are going to use that principle and try how best we can uh minimize

impact of all these pollutants on the environment and it is a more eco-friendly green alternative to conventional chemistry uh practices there are certain practices which have been going on for so long but now we are talking of green alternative
to those practices. And it also, of course, provides sustainable development, sustainable businesses, and sustainable living practices.

So as I mentioned, there are twelve principles of green chemistry. Prevent waste, atom economy, safe synthesis, safe products, design benign chemicals, design for energy efficiency, use of renewable feed stocks, reduce derivatives, catalysis,
Designed for degradation, pollution prevention, and accident prevention. Now let us look at each one of them and understand what the principle stands for. First

Prevent waste. Of course the first thing we have to talk about uh when we talk about pollution is that not to generate waste in the first place because once the waste is produced that it involves an extra cost and time to treat and safely dispose it.
And therefore the production cost also increases. So what we have to keep in mind here is that we synthesize only targeted product and minimum or no byproducts or waste material.
The second principle is atom economy. Now, what does it mean that synthetic methods should be used

In fact, in such a way the design should be of any reaction should be such that all the materials, in fact all the atoms which are present in the reactants should be incorporated into the products. That is atom economy. Now earlier

The emphasis was more on yield. Yes, here also we want a good yield, but at the same time it is not just the yield we are interested in. We want that all the atoms so that there is no uh extra atoms which are not being used or getting wasted.

So all the atoms in the reactants have to be included into the products, and this can be calculated for each reaction using this relationship. So percentage atom economy is equal to formula weight of the atoms which have been utilized and the

formula weight of all the reactants which have been used. So formula weight of atoms utilized divided by the formula weight of all reactants multiplied by 100 would give us the atom economy. Now let us take up some reactions. Like for example there's a substitution reaction. So what we are doing
Some of the atoms are getting substituted by another atom. So this would result in a moderate atom economy.

Whereas if there was an elimination reaction, definitely some small molecules are getting eliminated and or even uh larger molecules sometimes and then what happens to your atom economy? It has become low. If you have an addition reaction, we know that

Suppose there's a double bond and the reactants are getting incorporated into it, yes then we get hundred percent atom economy, and even if there is a rearrangement reaction again uh it is just rearrangement of the atoms which is taking place again we have a hundred percent atom economy. So if you have
Talking of green synthesis, then of course we understand atom economy must be maximum, and that is 100%.
Safer synthesis is the third principle. Now synthetic processes should be such that they are designed such a way to minimize or prevent the production of hazardous substances.

As far as possible, we should use only uh substances which are innocuous and necessary safety precautions have to be taken while processing to protect human health and the environment. For example, polyurethane

Now safe products. Now chemical products should be designed in such a way that the efficacy is preserved.
It functions as efficiency and as efficiently, but the toxicity is reduced. Now many of these products are generally found to have side effects. Now if we can think of ways

or in pharmaceuticals this plays a very important role because many of these drugs which are being used for as medicine we know that there is lot of side effects. So if they can be effective to

Then design benign chemicals. Now what happens is many of these chemical reactions we know are s uh carried out in a solvent medium.

Green chemistry

Class 50 content: 
Green chemistry: Introduction, twelve principles of green chemistry with examples

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Definition

   ‘Green Chemistry’ is the utilization of a set of principles that reduces or eliminates the use or generation of hazardous substances in the design, manufacture and application of products
			-Paul T. Anastas and John C. Warner

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Green Chemistry focuses on :

Reduction, recycling and/or eliminating toxic substances
Finding creative, alternative routes to minimize impact on the environment
More eco-friendly green alternative to conventional chemistry practices
Provides sustainable development, sustainable business and sustainable living practices

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Twelve Principles of Green Chemistry

Prevent Waste | Use of renewable feedstocks

Atom Economy | Reduce Derivatives

Safer Synthesis | Catalysis

Safe Products | Design for Degradation

Design Benign Chemicals | Pollution prevention

Design for Energy Efficiency | Accident Prevention

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Prevent Waste :
 Synthesis only targeted product with minimum or no 
   by products/waste

 If waste is produced , it involves cost and time to treat and safely dispose it, as a result production cost increases

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Atom Economy :
 Synthetic methods should be 
designed to maximize the incorporation of all materials used into the final product
The chemical processes should have maximum product yield
Atom economy can be calculated using the relation
% Atom Economy = (FW of atoms utilized/FW of all reactants) X 100
                      Atom Economy in a Substitution Reaction - moderate
                      Atom Economy in Elimination Reactions - low
                      Atom Economy in Addition Reactions -100% 
                      Atom Economy in Rearrangement Reactions -100%
For a green synthesis atom economy must be maximum (100%)

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Safer Synthesis :

The synthetic processes should be 
designed so as to minimize or prevent the production of hazardous substances 
Necessary safety precautions have to be taken while processing to protect human health and environment

e.g.,
  Polyurethane is manufactured conventionally using isocyanate and alcohol. However, isocyanate is  produced using  phosgene, a toxic gas 

 The alternative method by green synthesis of polyurethane eliminates the use of phosgene and uses CO2

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Safe Products :
  Chemical products should be designed
 to preserve efficacy of function while reducing toxicity  
Products should not have any side effects on the people using it and on the environment
It is envisaged to produce the chemical products specially those being used in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, etc.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Design Benign Chemicals :
Use safer solvents and reaction conditions
Avoid using solvents, separation agents, or other auxiliary chemicals
If these chemicals are necessary, use innocuous chemicals
Chemical syntheses are assisted by solvent medium: 
 recommended to use alternative solvents , greener in nature such as aqueous medium, liquid carbon-dioxide, ionic liquids(N-alkyl pyridinium cation with BF4- ) , or solvent free systems 
 Avoid harmful solvents like chloroform, pyridine which are known to cause health hazard, are carcinogenic to human beings and animals or cause severe damage to environment

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Design for Energy efficiency :
              Chemical processes are to be designed in such a way
              that they are less energy intensive 
    reactions occurring at mild conditions 
    require less time to complete

For this purpose it is worthwhile to utilize 
Bio-catalyst, homogeneous and heterogeneous catalyst which reduces the energy of activation 
Modern techniques such as solvent free synthesis, supercritical fluid systems, microwave irradiation, and ultrasound

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Use of renewable feedstock :
 Raw material or feedstock used as starting material should be renewable rather than depleting wherever technically and economically possible

Use of renewable feedstock such as biomass and agricultural wastes are strongly recommended rather than using non-renewable resources such as coal, petroleum-based raw materials, etc.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Reduce Derivatives :
 Avoid unnecessary derivatization 
temporary modification should be avoided whenever possible as they generate waste
the atom efficiency is reduced as the protective group is not incorporated in the final product
e.g. blocking group, protection/ deprotection

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Catalysis :
 Use catalytic reactions, as catalysts
Speed up the reaction
can be recycled and are highly selective 
less energy consumption during reaction
 obtaining high yield of product of high purity

Unlike stiochiometric reactions which are energy intensive require excessive reagents

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Design for Degradation :
 Design chemicals and products to degrade after use to innocuous substances after use so that they do not accumulate in the environment
Especially applicable to 
insecticides
pesticides 
polymers 
which tend to persist in the environment and  are known to cause bioaccumulations

Green chemistry

Every year we produce millions of tons of garbage which we dispose off in landfills













Waste disposal problems of these traditional plastics which are resistant to microbial degradation causes them to accumulate in the environment which is a serious threat to global ecology

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY

Biodegradable polymers: Polymers that can be decomposed by the action of microorganisms into water, carbon dioxide, methane and biomass
Biodegradation is a two step process:
The first step is fragmentation where the polymer  macromolecule is broken down into smaller chains or monomers by hydrolysis or oxidation
The second step is mineralisation by microorganisms .The products are CO2, CH4, H2O or biomass depending on the structure of the fragmented polymer chains and the environment they are exposed to

Source:https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/macp.202000017

Green chemistry

The susceptibility of a polymer to undergo degradation depends on :

The structure of the polymer, molecular weight, degree of branching, crystallinity and solubility
Usually polyesters, polyamides, polyurethanes  are found to be biodegradable

The environmental conditions like pH, availability of O2, light, temperature, humidity, microorganism etc.

Due to a large fraction of surface atoms compared to bulk.

the number of bonds need to be broken per atom during melting is less in nanomaterials

Nanomaterials

    Electrical conductivity decreases for nanoparticles as compared to bulk material
Due to spatial confinement
The electronic bands in bulk material are continuous
 In nano size materials the electronic bands become discrete and the band gap increases  
Some metals which are good conductors in bulk become semiconductors and insulators as their size is decreased to nano range

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Presence of polar groups in the polymer chain results
  in strong secondary force of attraction between the
  chains making them stiff and inflexible 

 Non polar groups have weak van der Waal’s
  attraction between them and hence they are more
  elastic 

 Presence of bulky, aromatic and cyclic groups in the
  polymer decreases the elasticity of the polymer

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

In elastic materials such as natural rubber, elasticity can  be improved by introducing cross linking at suitable molecular positions like in vulcanisation






In non-elastic materials, elasticity is achieved by using plasticisers , for example (Ph3PO4), which enter between the polymer chains and make a hard polymer more flexible

Source:https://revision4gcses.wordpress.com/science/chemistry-2/polymers/

Source:https://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1312811/FULLTEXT01.pdf

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Chemical resistance:
 Resistance to swell, dissolve and get degraded in the presence of a solvent or chemical
It depends on the chemical nature of monomeric units and their molecular arrangement

 Presence of polar and non-polar groups: Like dissolves like - A polymer is more soluble in a solvent of similar chemical structure 
Polymers having polar groups (–OH or –COOH groups) are usually attacked or dissolved by polar liquids such as water or alcohols. (e.g. PVA dissolves in water)
Polymers with non-polar groups such as –CH3 and –C6H5 are not easily attacked by polar solvents but they easily swell and sometimes dissolve in non-polar solvents such as petrol, benzene and carbon tetrachloride

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Residual unsaturation leads to oxidative degradation: polymers with residual double bonds get attacked and degraded in air and UV light 
 e.g.,natural rubber

Source:https://www.embibe.com/study/natural-rubber-vulcanization-of-natural-rubber-concept?entity_code=KTBP50

Packing: Dense packing does not allow the solvent to penetrate between the layers hence resistance increases, for example Teflon



Molecular mass: For a given polymer, the swelling character decreases with the increase in the molecular mass
 Degree of cross linking: Greater the degree of cross linking lesser is the solubility

Source:https://pslc.ws/macrog/ptfe.htm

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Plastic deformation :
 Property of a polymer by which on application of heat it becomes soft and flexible and on cooling it becomes hard and brittle is called plasticity or plastic deformation 

Based on their response to heat two kinds of polymers are:
 Thermoplastic - A thermoplastic polymer is one which softens on heating and becomes hard on cooling. It can be remoulded into new shapes, e.g., Polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene

Thermosetting - A thermosetting polymer becomes hard on heating. It cannot be remoulded, its structure instead undergoes a total degradation on heating, e.g.,Bakelite, Aniline aldehyde resin, urea formaldehyde resin

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

The reason for the difference in the thermal behaviour is:

Thermoplastics have relatively weak forces of attraction like van der Waals forces, dipole-dipole attraction or H-bonding between the chains, which are overcome when the material is heated

 Thermosetting plastics have the cross-linking between the chains is by strong covalent bonds cannot be broken easily. On strong heating will result in charring and degradation

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY

Polymethyl Methacrylate (PMMA) or Plexi Glass

It is an addition polymer
Plexi glass is obtained by radical polymerization in bulk, emulsion or suspension from the monomer methyl methacrylate (MMA)
Hydrogen peroxide is used as initiator
The monomer is obtained from acetone.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Properties 
It’s Tg 1050 C, colourless, transparent hard solid at room temperature.
Amorphous due the presence of bulky groups
Resistant to many chemicals but soluble in organic solvent like acetone and chlorinated hydrocarbons and esters 
Higher the optical clarity (100% Transparent in visible light radiation) 
It has a good dimensional stability

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Applications

Due to its optical clarity it is used to make aircraft windows, signal boards etc
For Making artificial teeth and contact lens
Used in paints and adhesives
Making transparent bottles and wash basins.
Good substitute for glass but has poor scratch resistance.

Average molecular weight of polymers - number average, weight average, and viscosity average molecular weight; numerical problems

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Molecular weight of Polymers
Polymers are a mix of chains of different lengths
Weight of polymers is expressed as an average molecular weight
The molecular weight is an important characteristic of a polymer sample as several properties of polymers depend on the molecular weight
The entire range of mechanical properties like stress-strain, impact, fracture, fatigue, creep, stress relaxation and cracking are influenced by average molecular weight and molecular weight distribution

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Number average molecular weight

Weight average molecular weight

Average molecular weight

Viscosity average molecular weight

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Number average molecular weight, 
 Obtained by dividing the total weight of the dispersed material with the total number of polymer units present

where n1, n2, n3 …. are number of polymer units having molecular weights M1, M2, M3,…. respectively

where ni is the number of polymer units of molecular mass Mi
It depends only on number of polymer units and not their size
Colligative properties like osmotic pressure, elevation in  boiling point or depression in melting point is used to determine number average molecular weight

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Weight average molecular weight, 

   It gives representation to various molecular species in
    proportion to their masses in the given material
   In the averaging process, the molecular weight of each
    individual species is multiplied by its mass

where m1, m2, m3 …. are masses of polymer units having molecular weights M1, M2, M3 respectively

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

if n1, n2, n3 …. are number of polymer units having
   molecular weights M1, M2, M3 respectively 
  then m1 = n1M1, m2 = n2 M2 ….
 Weight average molecular weight can be written as





  It depends on size of the polymer units
  Properties which depend on size like sedimentation
   velocity or light scattering are used to determine weight
   average molecular weight

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

The ratio            is called the polydispersity index (PDI) 
 
It is a measure for the broadness of a molecular weight distribution of a polymer, that is, the larger the polydispersity index, the broader the molecular weight distribution
A monodisperse polymer where all the chain lengths are equal has  PDI =1
PDI > 1, shows that the polymeric sample is less homogeneous and polydisperse

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY (UE26CY151 A,B)

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Class 48 content: 
Conducting polymers - examples, types of doping

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Conducting polymers

Polymers are generally insulators because the organic molecules of which they are composed have no free electrons to carry current

An organic polymer with highly delocalized pi-electron system, having electrical conductance of the order of an electrical conductor is called a conducting polymer

Also known as synthetic metals

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Development :

1977 - Heeger, Macdiarmid & Shirakawa demonstrated conductivity of polyacetylene can be increased 13 times by doping with electron acceptors and donors

Norman et. al - achieved conductance of polyacetylene equal to copper

Doping with less than 10% of chemical species results in dramatic changes in electrical, electronic, magnetic and optical properties of polymers – hence it is a new class of polymers

2000 - Heeger, Macdiarmid & Shirakawa won the Nobel prize for Chemistry

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Examples of polymers which conduct after doping

[Image text, OCR]
Polyacetylene
Polyphenylene
Polyprrrole
Polythiophene
Polyaniline
Poly(phenyl ene
-vinylene)

Source:https://www.researchgate.net/figure/3Molecular-structure-of-some-typical-conducting-polymers_fig2_304023062

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Conducting polymers conduct electricity due to delocalization of π electrons 
An organic polymer can be converted into conducting polymer if it has :
• linear structure
• extensive conjugation in its polymeric back bone

POLYACETYLENE

POLYPHENYLENE

Source:https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Some-Examples-for-Conducting-Polymers_fig4_269993677

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

These materials in pure form are not conductors but on doping (Introduction of charged chemical species) conduction increases

Types of Doping

Oxidative doping

Reductive doping

Proton doping

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Oxidative doping (p-doping) 
In this process, pi-backbone of a polymer is partially oxidized using a suitable oxidizing agent 
This creates positively charged sites on the polymer backbone which are the current carriers for conduction 
The oxidizing agents used are Iodine in CCl4, HBF4 etc.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Reductive doping (n-doping) :
 In this process, pi-backbone of a polymer is partially reduced using a suitable reducing agent 
This creates negatively charged sites on the polymer backbone which are the current carriers for conduction 
The reducing agent used is sodium naphthalide in THF

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Protonic acid doping :
 In this technique, current carrying charged species (+ve and –ve) are created by using a protonic acid as dopant

 Doping of polyaniline is a typical example of this type of doping

Conducting polymers

Polymers are generally insulators because the organic molecules of which they are composed have no free electrons to carry current

An organic polymer with highly delocalized pi-electron system, having electrical conductance of the order of an electrical conductor is called a conducting polymer

Also known as synthetic metals

Functional materials - Polymers

Development :

1977 - Heeger, Macdiarmid & Shirakawa demonstrated conductivity of polyacetylene can be increased 13 times by doping with electron acceptors and donors

Norman et. al - achieved conductance of polyacetylene equal to copper

Doping with less than 10% of chemical species results in dramatic changes in electrical, electronic, magnetic and optical properties of polymers – hence it is a new class of polymers

2000 - Heeger, Macdiarmid & Shirakawa won the Nobel prize for Chemistry

Oxidative doping (p-doping) 
In this process, pi-backbone of a polymer is partially oxidized using a suitable oxidizing agent 
This creates positively charged sites on the polymer backbone which are the current carriers for conduction 
The oxidizing agents used are Iodine in CCl4, HBF4 etc.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Reductive doping (n-doping) :
 In this process, pi-backbone of a polymer is partially reduced using a suitable reducing agent 
This creates negatively charged sites on the polymer backbone which are the current carriers for conduction 
The reducing agent used is sodium naphthalide in THF

 In this technique, current carrying charged species (+ve and –ve) are created by using a protonic acid as dopant

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY (UE26CY151 A,B)

Department of Science and Humanities

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Class 50 content: 
Green chemistry: Introduction, twelve principles of green chemistry with examples

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Definition

   ‘Green Chemistry’ is the utilization of a set of principles that reduces or eliminates the use or generation of hazardous substances in the design, manufacture and application of products
			-Paul T. Anastas and John C. Warner

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Green Chemistry focuses on :

Reduction, recycling and/or eliminating toxic substances
Finding creative, alternative routes to minimize impact on the environment
More eco-friendly green alternative to conventional chemistry practices
Provides sustainable development, sustainable business and sustainable living practices

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Twelve Principles of Green Chemistry

Prevent Waste | Use of renewable feedstocks

Atom Economy | Reduce Derivatives

Safer Synthesis | Catalysis

Safe Products | Design for Degradation

Design Benign Chemicals | Pollution prevention

Design for Energy Efficiency | Accident Prevention

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Prevent Waste :
 Synthesis only targeted product with minimum or no 
   by products/waste

 If waste is produced , it involves cost and time to treat and safely dispose it, as a result production cost increases

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Atom Economy :
 Synthetic methods should be 
designed to maximize the incorporation of all materials used into the final product
The chemical processes should have maximum product yield
Atom economy can be calculated using the relation
% Atom Economy = (FW of atoms utilized/FW of all reactants) X 100
                      Atom Economy in a Substitution Reaction - moderate
                      Atom Economy in Elimination Reactions - low
                      Atom Economy in Addition Reactions -100% 
                      Atom Economy in Rearrangement Reactions -100%
For a green synthesis atom economy must be maximum (100%)

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Safer Synthesis :

The synthetic processes should be 
designed so as to minimize or prevent the production of hazardous substances 
Necessary safety precautions have to be taken while processing to protect human health and environment

e.g.,
  Polyurethane is manufactured conventionally using isocyanate and alcohol. However, isocyanate is  produced using  phosgene, a toxic gas 

 The alternative method by green synthesis of polyurethane eliminates the use of phosgene and uses CO2

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Safe Products :
  Chemical products should be designed
 to preserve efficacy of function while reducing toxicity  
Products should not have any side effects on the people using it and on the environment
It is envisaged to produce the chemical products specially those being used in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, etc.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Design Benign Chemicals :
Use safer solvents and reaction conditions
Avoid using solvents, separation agents, or other auxiliary chemicals
If these chemicals are necessary, use innocuous chemicals
Chemical syntheses are assisted by solvent medium: 
 recommended to use alternative solvents , greener in nature such as aqueous medium, liquid carbon-dioxide, ionic liquids(N-alkyl pyridinium cation with BF4- ) , or solvent free systems 
 Avoid harmful solvents like chloroform, pyridine which are known to cause health hazard, are carcinogenic to human beings and animals or cause severe damage to environment

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Design for Energy efficiency :
              Chemical processes are to be designed in such a way
              that they are less energy intensive 
    reactions occurring at mild conditions 
    require less time to complete

For this purpose it is worthwhile to utilize 
Bio-catalyst, homogeneous and heterogeneous catalyst which reduces the energy of activation 
Modern techniques such as solvent free synthesis, supercritical fluid systems, microwave irradiation, and ultrasound

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Use of renewable feedstock :
 Raw material or feedstock used as starting material should be renewable rather than depleting wherever technically and economically possible

Use of renewable feedstock such as biomass and agricultural wastes are strongly recommended rather than using non-renewable resources such as coal, petroleum-based raw materials, etc.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Reduce Derivatives :
 Avoid unnecessary derivatization 
temporary modification should be avoided whenever possible as they generate waste
the atom efficiency is reduced as the protective group is not incorporated in the final product
e.g. blocking group, protection/ deprotection

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Catalysis :
 Use catalytic reactions, as catalysts
Speed up the reaction
can be recycled and are highly selective 
less energy consumption during reaction
 obtaining high yield of product of high purity

Unlike stiochiometric reactions which are energy intensive require excessive reagents

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Design for Degradation :
 Design chemicals and products to degrade after use to innocuous substances after use so that they do not accumulate in the environment
Especially applicable to 
insecticides
pesticides 
polymers 
which tend to persist in the environment and  are known to cause bioaccumulations

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Biodegradable Polymers
Every year we produce millions of tons of garbage which we dispose off in landfills













Waste disposal problems of these traditional plastics which are resistant to microbial degradation causes them to accumulate in the environment which is a serious threat to global ecology

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Biodegradable polymers: Polymers that can be decomposed by the action of microorganisms into water, carbon dioxide, methane and biomass
Biodegradation is a two step process:
The first step is fragmentation where the polymer  macromolecule is broken down into smaller chains or monomers by hydrolysis or oxidation
The second step is mineralisation by microorganisms .The products are CO2, CH4, H2O or biomass depending on the structure of the fragmented polymer chains and the environment they are exposed to

Source:https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/macp.202000017

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

The susceptibility of a polymer to undergo degradation depends on :

The structure of the polymer, molecular weight, degree of branching, crystallinity and solubility
Usually polyesters, polyamides, polyurethanes  are found to be biodegradable

The environmental conditions like pH, availability of O2, light, temperature, humidity, microorganism etc.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Examples of Biodegradable polymers

Abbreviation | Name of the polymer

PVOH | Polyvinyl Alcohol

PLA | Polylactic acid

PHB | Polyhydroxybutyrate

PHBV | Poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate)

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Pollution Prevention :
 Real-time analysis (quality control)
 Continuously monitor and control the formation of hazardous substances
Any unreacted reactant can be recycled in order to minimize the use of chemicals

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Accident Prevention :
 Minimize the potential for accidents
Chemicals chosen for processes should be such which minimise accidents in the form of fires, explosions, and toxic releases to the environment 
Manufacturing plants should be well equipped with safety mechanisms

The Bhopal gas tragedy is one of the worst industrial disasters

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Green chemistry is a set of principles which emphasises on 
environmentally benign chemical synthesis with a view to devise pathways for the prevention of pollution

 bringing a paradigm shift in chemical processing to achieve sustainable development

			-Paul T. Anastas and John C. Warner

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Green Chemistry focuses on :

Reduction, recycling and/or eliminating toxic substances
Finding creative, alternative routes to minimize impact on the environment
More eco-friendly green alternative to conventional chemistry practices
Provides sustainable development, sustainable business and sustainable living practices

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Twelve Principles of Green Chemistry

Prevent Waste | Use of renewable feedstocks

Atom Economy | Reduce Derivatives

Safer Synthesis | Catalysis

Safe Products | Design for Degradation

Design Benign Chemicals | Pollution prevention

Design for Energy Efficiency | Accident Prevention

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Prevent Waste :
 Synthesis only targeted product with minimum or no 
   by products/waste

 If waste is produced , it involves cost and time to treat and safely dispose it, as a result production cost increases

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Atom Economy :
 Synthetic methods should be 
designed to maximize the incorporation of all materials used into the final product
The chemical processes should have maximum product yield
Atom economy can be calculated using the relation
% Atom Economy = (FW of atoms utilized/FW of all reactants) X 100
                      Atom Economy in a Substitution Reaction - moderate
                      Atom Economy in Elimination Reactions - low
                      Atom Economy in Addition Reactions -100% 
                      Atom Economy in Rearrangement Reactions -100%
For a green synthesis atom economy must be maximum (100%)

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Safer Synthesis :

The synthetic processes should be 
designed so as to minimize or prevent the production of hazardous substances 
Necessary safety precautions have to be taken while processing to protect human health and environment

e.g.,
  Polyurethane is manufactured conventionally using isocyanate and alcohol. However, isocyanate is  produced using  phosgene, a toxic gas 

 The alternative method by green synthesis of polyurethane eliminates the use of phosgene and uses CO2

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Safe Products :
  Chemical products should be designed
 to preserve efficacy of function while reducing toxicity  
Products should not have any side effects on the people using it and on the environment
It is envisaged to produce the chemical products specially those being used in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, etc.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Design Benign Chemicals :
Use safer solvents and reaction conditions
Avoid using solvents, separation agents, or other auxiliary chemicals
If these chemicals are necessary, use innocuous chemicals
Chemical syntheses are assisted by solvent medium: 
 recommended to use alternative solvents , greener in nature such as aqueous medium, liquid carbon-dioxide, ionic liquids(N-alkyl pyridinium cation with BF4- ) , or solvent free systems 
 Avoid harmful solvents like chloroform, pyridine which are known to cause health hazard, are carcinogenic to human beings and animals or cause severe damage to environment

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Design for Energy efficiency :
              Chemical processes are to be designed in such a way
              that they are less energy intensive 
    reactions occurring at mild conditions 
    require less time to complete

For this purpose it is worthwhile to utilize 
Bio-catalyst, homogeneous and heterogeneous catalyst which reduces the energy of activation 
Modern techniques such as solvent free synthesis, supercritical fluid systems, microwave irradiation, and ultrasound

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Use of renewable feedstock :
 Raw material or feedstock used as starting material should be renewable rather than depleting wherever technically and economically possible

Use of renewable feedstock such as biomass and agricultural wastes are strongly recommended rather than using non-renewable resources such as coal, petroleum-based raw materials, etc.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Reduce Derivatives :
 Avoid unnecessary derivatization 
temporary modification should be avoided whenever possible as they generate waste
the atom efficiency is reduced as the protective group is not incorporated in the final product
e.g. blocking group, protection/ deprotection

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Catalysis :
 Use catalytic reactions, as catalysts
Speed up the reaction
can be recycled and are highly selective 
less energy consumption during reaction
 obtaining high yield of product of high purity

Unlike stiochiometric reactions which are energy intensive require excessive reagents

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Design for Degradation :
 Design chemicals and products to degrade after use to innocuous substances after use so that they do not accumulate in the environment
Especially applicable to 
insecticides
pesticides 
polymers 
which tend to persist in the environment and  are known to cause bioaccumulations

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Green chemistry

Biodegradable Polymers
Every year we produce millions of tons of garbage which we dispose off in landfills













Waste disposal problems of these traditional plastics which are resistant to microbial degradation causes them to accumulate in the environment which is a serious threat to global ecology

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY

Biodegradable polymers: Polymers that can be decomposed by the action of microorganisms into water, carbon dioxide, methane and biomass
Biodegradation is a two step process:
The first step is fragmentation where the polymer  macromolecule is broken down into smaller chains or monomers by hydrolysis or oxidation
The second step is mineralisation by microorganisms .The products are CO2, CH4, H2O or biomass depending on the structure of the fragmented polymer chains and the environment they are exposed to

Source:https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/macp.202000017

Green chemistry

The susceptibility of a polymer to undergo degradation depends on :

The structure of the polymer, molecular weight, degree of branching, crystallinity and solubility
Usually polyesters, polyamides, polyurethanes  are found to be biodegradable

The environmental conditions like pH, availability of O2, light, temperature, humidity, microorganism etc.

Manufacturing plants should be well equipped with safety mechanisms

transcript_segments.text: Good morning, and
welcome to Electronic Principles and Devices.
Today we are going to learn about
unit one. In that, topic one,
an introduction to semiconductor.
So semiconductors are special class of elements, having a conductivity between that
of a good conductor and that of an insulator.
The three semiconductors which is most commonly or most frequently used in the
construction of electronic devices are germanium, silicon, and gallium arsenide.
And we also see that the atomic structure of silicon and germanium.
First, if you look at the atomic structure of silicon, the atomic number is 14, and
it's represented in terms of SPDF model one S two, two S two, two P six, three S
two.
And if you start arranging with respect to the shell around,
we call it as orbits. So the first orbit can have two, second can have eight,
and the remaining four, that is three S two, three P two are at the outside.
We call it as a valence shell, which has four valence electron.
Similarly, any semiconductor material, if you look at example again, germanium
32, the outermost valence electron will be four again.
That means to say,
they are not stable. So they themselves will try to be stable
with the help of a bond called covalent bond.
But before that, they
try to balance by themselves by moving from lower energy level to the higher energy
level. So semiconductor in comparison with an insulator, if you look at, there is a
large energy gap between the conduction band and the valence band in the case of an
insulator. There is a no gap at all.
There's an overlapping in the case of a conductor between the conduction band and
the valence band. Whereas in the case of a semiconductor, as we see, there is a
little gap compared to the insulator and conductor.
So they could, with a change in the temperature or with the applied voltage, the
charges will start move from lower energy level to higher energy level.
So keeping this in mind now,
if you go back, the outermost valence electron, they try to move from lower band to
higher band.
So the
semiconductor has been classified into intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductor.
The term intrinsic is applied to any semiconductor material that carefully refine
to reduce the number of impurities to a very low level.
That is, we can call it as a pure form, made available through modern technology.
Whereas extrinsic semiconductor are those that can be subjected to doping process
with the impurities being added to that.
So as we see the structure of silicon with,
as we see here, it's having an outermost four valence bond, forming a covalent bond
by sharing of an electron with a neighboring.
Even in the upper part, even in the lower, even in the lower and also the side we
see that there is a covalent bond where valence electrons are shared.
So this is the concept on which the semiconductor working principle depends
on. With the increase in the voltage, the semiconductor act like a conductor where
covalent bond is ruptured, with the temperature reduced
act like an insulator where the covalent bonds are not ruptured.
So keeping this in mind now,
these extrinsic semiconductor has been classified based on the impurity level
added. For example, if you look at the first diagram here, as marked here, where
the impurity added is the antimony impurity has been added, where outermost five
valence electrons are there. We know the four valence electrons are shared with the
neighboring silicon atom, and one is free,
the fifth valence electron of the antimony is free.
And if you apply the voltage to this
bonding arrangement, and covalent bond is ruptured, one more electrons will get
free up. So there are two
free electrons with one hole left over.
That means the number of electrons are more compared to the holes here.
So electrons are N-type. So the type of the
structure obtained is N-type material, which is created by introducing the impurity
element that have five valence electron pentavalent, and this could be possible
with the addition of an impurity such as antimony, arsenic, and phosphorus.
Similarly, if I look at
here, there is a structure which has a boron as an impurity introduced here
with three valence electron, if the trivalent impurity has been added and one is
void. No covalent bond is formed, so already there exists one bond.
With the addition of an impurity over there,
results in one hole. With the further
change, means you say with applied voltage, one more covalent bond is ruptured, and
a free electron is released and a hole is introduced over there.
So there are two holes and one electron where the number of hole charges are more.
The positive charge material is formed with the introduction of a trivalent
impurity with the three valence electron such as boron, gallium, and indium
materials.
Next,
let us see what is a diode, where diode is one which has a two airports.
We can construct our first solid state electronic device, that is a semiconductor
diode, by sandwiching P-type and N-type material together to form a depletion
region between the two. It is
a fabrication of one material with majority charge carrier of
electron to one with majority carrier of holes.
How do we do a biasing of a diode?
Where we go for forward bias and reverse bias.
In a forward bias, a material type connected to the same polarity
terminal of a voltage source. Whereas the reverse bias, a material type connected
to a opposite polarity terminal of the voltage source.
As shown in the diagram now, a P-type and N-type material sandwich with the
depletion region form. Now a P-type is connected to the same material, that is
P terminal and a N
region is connected to the negative terminal, then it's said to be the forward
bias. And if you reverse this, it's called as a reverse bias.
We see the different type of diodes in the diagram here.
Various companies have come up with the various
structures of diodes here as we see.
It could be a two terminal or a three terminal also sometime.
So that could depend on the company and even the representation here, we see
the normal resistor like or a
IC-based
diodes, which could be designed by the different companies.
Thank you.

transcript_segments.text: Good morning, and welcome back
to Electronic Principles and Devices.
Today we will go with the topic three, Introduction to Semiconductor
Diode.
In the last class we have looked at the diode and biasing of the diode,
where we know that diode has two regions, P and N type, where P side is connected
with the biasing. P side is connected to the positive of the terminal and N side is
connected to negative of the battery terminal.
Now before we go understanding about the biasing part, let us understand the basic
principle and concept of bias and no bias.
So as we see here in the diagram, we have a no bias setup with a
P
and N region not connected to the voltage supply. We call it as a no bias.
So in the absence of an applied bias across the semiconductor diode, the net flow
of charges in one direction is zero.
That means to say, with no voltage applied to the diode, we see that the boundary,
there is a depletion region with the charges being accumulated.
This happens
because at the instant the two metals are joined, the electrons and the holes in
the region of the junction will combine, resulting in lack of free charges in the
region near the junction, as shown, which we call it as a depletion region.
And note in the figure that only particle displayed in this region are positive and
negative ion remaining once the free charges have been observed.
That means to say, because of the concentration gradient, the charge carriers will
start move from
P side to N side and N side to P side. As the moment they
start moving, they forms a charges
which is been settled at the boundaries of the P and N,
where negative charge is settled at the P region boundary and
positive charge is settled at the N region boundary.
This region of uncovered positive and negative ion is called depletion region.
This is due to the depletion of free charge
carrier in the region. So which we call it as a no bias condition.
Now let us go with forward bias. As the name indicates, a forward bias or
'ON' condition. The current that exists under the forward bias is called the
forward bias current and is represented by ID in the diagram.
As the name indicates, forward bias, we connect P region to positive terminal of
the battery and N region to negative terminal of the battery.
As the moment we connect it, we call it as an 'ON' condition, that is
established by applying a positive potential to the P terminal and a negative
potential to the N terminal, as shown in the diagram.
The application of the forward bias potential that is VD we call here, will
pressurize or will pressure the electron in the N-type material and hole in the
P-type material to recombine with ion near the boundary and reduces the width
of the depletion region, as shown here.
If compared to the previous diagram, we have a very big depletion region which is
shown here. And because of the application of the voltage, the depletion region is
reduced and we see only a few charge carrier.
This happens due to the application of the voltage on both P and N region, and
which results in the ID current which is a sum of the eye majority and the leakage
current.
This can be represented by a V-A characteristic, as shown, the forward bias current
is shown here. There is a very less resistance is there in the forward bias and we
see that there is a current flow with application of the voltage.
This is about the forward bias. Then what is reverse bias?
The reverse bias condition, the P side is connected to the negative terminal of the
battery, N side is connected to the positive terminal of the battery with applied
voltage VD.
So when a PN junction is reverse biased, the number of uncovered positive ions in
the depletion region of the N-type material
will increase, as shown here. It's increasing due to the large number of free
electron drawn from the positive terminal of the applied voltage.
Similarly, the negative terminal of the applied voltage here.
For a similar reason, the number of uncovered ion will increase in the P-type
material. The net effect therefore is widening of a depletion region, as shown.
This widening of the depletion region will establish too a great
a barrier for majority carrier to overcome, effectively reducing the majority
carrier flow to zero.
So the current that exists under a reverse bias condition is called the reverse
saturation current and is represented as IS.
And this also represented in the V-A characteristic as shown, with the initial
applied voltage because of the depletion region will not be able to see the current
flow which has been
shown here. And once after the reverse breakdown region, once after the
voltage called VBR, there is going to be a breakdown with the current increase
as shown.
And this could be
realized from a reverse bias condition.
So today's class we have seen with a no bias condition, forward bias condition and
a reverse bias condition. Thank you.

transcript_segments.text: Good morning, and welcome to Electronic Principle and Devices.
I'm Professor Ananda, Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering.
Today, we are going to see the semiconductor diode characteristics and parameters
and with some numericals.
So, as we see in the previous class, the diode characteristics, we have seen the
forward and the reverse bias characteristics.
As we look at the forward bias here,
initially for the applied voltage, the diode was off,
and at particular voltage
of Vf, the current start increasing.
Similarly, in the reverse bias, as applied voltage is increased, at one particular
voltage, which is a breakdown voltage, the current start increasing.
So to understand this, let us
consider the characteristics once again with the I and V, where we call this region
as a forward bias, we call this region as a reverse bias.
So from the characteristics curve of the semiconductor diode, the following region
and parameter have been observed here.
So in a forward bias region,
the voltage at which the diode start conducting is called as a knee voltage.
So for a silicon, it is 0.7, for germanium it is 0.3.
So the voltage at which the diode start conducting is called a forward, as a knee
voltage. Then, we also come to another parameter called forward current rating.
The forward current rating, which is I.
It's the maximum current
at which the diode starts conducting.
It depends on the voltage at which the diode is on.
So for silicon, it's 0.7 volts, for germanium, it's 0.3.
So the current can vary based on the device, because it
depends on the fabrication of the device.
Then the maximum power expression P is equal to V into I.
So once we know the voltage and the current, we get the power value.
Similarly, coming to the reverse bias here,
the breakdown voltage plays important role. The first is breakdown voltage.
Until there is a breakdown, there is a leakage current flowing, which is a reverse
saturation current, which is
less than the reverse saturation current, which is called as
a leakage current. We need to remember this.
Then, the reverse saturation current is this region, where the diode start
conducting even with the reverse bias. That happens at a reverse bias voltage.
It could vary based on the device. It could be five volts reverse saturation
current. That depends on the fabrication again.
Then we also need to calculate what the peak inverse voltage, the voltage at which
the device starts conducting, which is a peak inverse voltage rating.
And the diode representation symbol is this, where it looks like an arrow lying
here. The arrow indicate the conventional current flow from P region to N region.
Next, we also learn here the diode current expression or the Shockley's current
equation. The Shockley's equation is also called as a
