MATLAB – Plotting

➢To plot the graph of a function, we need to take the following

   steps:

➢Define x, by specifying the range of values for the variable x, for

  which the function is to be plotted.

➢Define the function, y = f(x). Call the plot command, as plot(x, y).

➢The plot command is used to create two-dimensional plots.

➢Following example would demonstrate the concept.

➢Let us plot the function 𝑦= 3.5−0.5𝑥cos 6𝑥  for −2 ≤𝑥≤4.

MATLAB – Plotting, Continued…

 ➢The script file is as follows:

    >> x=[-2:0.01:4];  (Here 0.01 is the spacing value)

    >> y=3.5.^(-0.5*x).*cos(6*x);

    >> plot(x,y)

 ➢Here 𝑦is plotted as a function of 𝑥.

MATLAB – Plotting, Continued…

  ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following plot:

MATLAB – Plotting, Continued…

 ➢Let us take another example to plot the function 𝑦= 𝑥2.

 ➢In this example, we will draw two graphs with the same function, but

     in second time, we will reduce the value of increment.

 ➢Note   that as we decrease the increment, the graph becomes

    smoother.

 ➢The script file is as follows:

    >> x = [-100:20:100];

    >> y = x.^2;

    >> plot(x, y)

MATLAB – Plotting, Continued…

  ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following plot:

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots

 ➢Three-dimensional  plots  display a  surface defined by a

    function in two variables, 𝑔= 𝑓(𝑥, 𝑦).

 ➢To define the function 𝑔= 𝑓(𝑥, 𝑦), we first create a set of

     𝑥, 𝑦  points  over  the  domain  of  the  function  using

    the meshgrid command. Next, we assign the function itself.

     Finally, we use the surf command to create a surface plot.

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots, Continued…

 ➢The following example demonstrates the concept:
 ➢Let us create a 3D surface map for the function 𝑧= 𝑥𝑒−𝑥2+𝑦2

 ➢The script file is as follows:

   >> [x,y] = meshgrid(-2:.2:2);

    >> z = x.* exp(-x.^2 - y.^2);

    >> surf(x,y,z)

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots, Continued…

 ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following 3-D map:

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots, Continued…

 ➢Let us consider another example to create a 3D surface map for

    the function 𝑧= sinx + cosy

 ➢The script file is as follows:

   >> [x,y] = meshgrid(-2:.2:2);

   >> z=sin(x)+cos(y);

    >> surf(x,y,z)

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots, Continued…

 ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following 3-D map:

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots, Continued…

 ➢Let us consider another example to create a 3D surface map for

                 𝑥𝑦𝑥2−𝑦2
    the function 𝑧=                .                     𝑥2+𝑦2

 ➢The script file is as follows:

   >> [x,y] = meshgrid(-2:.2:2);

   >> z=x.*y.*(x.^2-y.^2)./(x.^2+y.^2);

   >> surf(x,y,z)

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots, Continued…

 ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following 3-D map:

Adding Title and Labels on the Graph

 ➢Using MATLAB we can add title, labels along the x-axis and

    y-axis of the graph.

 ➢The xlabel and ylabel commands generate labels along x-axis

   and y-axis.

 ➢The title command allows you to put a title on the graph.

 ➢The script file is as follows:

   >> x = [0:0.01:10];

   >> y = sin(x);

   >> plot(x, y), xlabel('x'), ylabel('Sin(x)'), title('Sin(x) Graph')

Adding Title and Labels on the Graph

 ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following plot:

MATLAB – Polar Plots

 ➢To plot a curve  in polar coordinates, we use the following

   command:

  ➢polarplot(theta,rho). Here theta is the angle in radians and rho is

    the radius value for each point.

 ➢Following example would demonstrate the concept.

 ➢Let us plot the curve 𝑟= 𝑠𝑖𝑛2𝜃𝑐𝑜𝑠2𝜃.

MATLAB – Polar Plots, Continued…


 ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following plot:

MATLAB – Polar Plots, Continued…


 ➢Consider another example:

 ➢Plot the curve 𝑟= 1 −𝑠𝑖𝑛𝜃

 ➢The script file is as follows:

   >> theta = 0:0.01:2*pi;

   >> rho = 1 - sin(theta);

   >> polar(theta, rho)

MATLAB – Polar Plots, Continued…

 ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following plot:

MATLAB – Polar Plots, Continued…


 ➢Consider another example:

 ➢Plot the curve 𝑟= 𝑐𝑜𝑠2𝜃

 ➢The script file is as follows:

    >> theta = 0:0.01:2*pi;

    >> rho = cos(2*theta);

    >> polar(theta, rho)

MATLAB – Polar Plots, Continued…

 ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following plot:

MATLAB – Parametric Plots

 ➢To plot a parametric curve, we use the following command:

  ➢fplot3(xt,yt,zt), which plots the parametric curve xt=x(t), yt=y(t),

    and zt=z(t) over the default interval −5 < 𝑡< 5.

 ➢Following example would demonstrate the concept.

 ➢Let us plot a parametric curve: x=sin(t); y=cos(t); z=t over the

    default parameter range [-5 5].

MATLAB – Parametric Plots, Continued…


 ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following plot:

MATLAB – Polar Plots, Continued…

 ➢Consider another example:


                                          10 ➢Plot the parametric curve 𝑥= 𝑒−𝑡 sin 5𝑡; 𝑦=



       10   𝑒−𝑡 cos 5𝑡; 𝑧= 𝑡

ENGINEERING MATHEMATICS-I
MATLAB


Department of Science and Humanities

MATLAB – Plotting

➢To plot the graph of a function, we need to take the following

   steps:

➢Define x, by specifying the range of values for the variable x, for

  which the function is to be plotted.

➢Define the function, y = f(x). Call the plot command, as plot(x, y).

➢The plot command is used to create two-dimensional plots.

➢Following example would demonstrate the concept.

➢Let us plot the function 𝑦= 3.5−0.5𝑥cos 6𝑥  for −2 ≤𝑥≤4.

MATLAB – Plotting, Continued…

 ➢The script file is as follows:

    >> x=[-2:0.01:4];  (Here 0.01 is the spacing value)

    >> y=3.5.^(-0.5*x).*cos(6*x);

    >> plot(x,y)

 ➢Here 𝑦is plotted as a function of 𝑥.

MATLAB – Plotting, Continued…

  ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following plot:

MATLAB – Plotting, Continued…

 ➢Let us take another example to plot the function 𝑦= 𝑥2.

 ➢In this example, we will draw two graphs with the same function, but

     in second time, we will reduce the value of increment.

 ➢Note   that as we decrease the increment, the graph becomes

    smoother.

 ➢The script file is as follows:

    >> x = [-100:20:100];

    >> y = x.^2;

    >> plot(x, y)

MATLAB – Plotting, Continued…

  ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following plot:

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots

 ➢Three-dimensional  plots  display a  surface defined by a

    function in two variables, 𝑔= 𝑓(𝑥, 𝑦).

 ➢To define the function 𝑔= 𝑓(𝑥, 𝑦), we first create a set of

     𝑥, 𝑦  points  over  the  domain  of  the  function  using

    the meshgrid command. Next, we assign the function itself.

     Finally, we use the surf command to create a surface plot.

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots, Continued…

 ➢The following example demonstrates the concept:
 ➢Let us create a 3D surface map for the function 𝑧= 𝑥𝑒−𝑥2+𝑦2

 ➢The script file is as follows:

   >> [x,y] = meshgrid(-2:.2:2);

    >> z = x.* exp(-x.^2 - y.^2);

    >> surf(x,y,z)

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots, Continued…

 ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following 3-D map:

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots, Continued…

 ➢Let us consider another example to create a 3D surface map for

    the function 𝑧= sinx + cosy

 ➢The script file is as follows:

   >> [x,y] = meshgrid(-2:.2:2);

   >> z=sin(x)+cos(y);

    >> surf(x,y,z)

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots, Continued…

 ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following 3-D map:

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots, Continued…

 ➢Let us consider another example to create a 3D surface map for

                 𝑥𝑦𝑥2−𝑦2
    the function 𝑧=                .                     𝑥2+𝑦2

 ➢The script file is as follows:

   >> [x,y] = meshgrid(-2:.2:2);

   >> z=x.*y.*(x.^2-y.^2)./(x.^2+y.^2);

   >> surf(x,y,z)

MATLAB - Three Dimensional Plots, Continued…

 ➢When we run the file, MATLAB displays the following 3-D map:

Adding Title and Labels on the Graph

 ➢Using MATLAB we can add title, labels along the x-axis and

    y-axis of the graph.

 ➢The xlabel and ylabel commands generate labels along x-axis

   and y-axis.

 ➢The title command allows you to put a title on the graph.

 ➢The script file is as follows:

   >> x = [0:0.01:10];

   >> y = sin(x);

   >> plot(x, y), xlabel('x'), ylabel('Sin(x)'), title('Sin(x) Graph')

Adding Title and Labels on the Graph

 ➢To plot a curve  in polar coordinates, we use the following

   command:

    the radius value for each point.

 ➢Following example would demonstrate the concept.

 ➢Let us plot the curve 𝑟= 𝑠𝑖𝑛2𝜃𝑐𝑜𝑠2𝜃.

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB
Introduction to MATLAB, Commands, Variables & Plotting

Introduction • Commands • Variables • 2D & 3D Plotting

1

2. Learning Objectives

• Identify the main parts of the MATLAB user interface.
• Use basic commands and assign values to variables.
• Create and customize 2D Cartesian and polar plots.
• Create introductory 3D curves and surfaces.
• Add titles, axis labels, legends, grids and curve labels.
• Modify and edit plots to communicate results clearly.

Goal: learn by typing, running, observing and changing MATLAB code.

2

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

3. What is MATLAB?

• MATLAB = MATrix LABoratory.
• A programming and numerical-computing environment used by engineers and scientists.
• Works naturally with vectors, matrices, equations, data and graphs.
• Provides built-in functions for mathematics, visualization, simulation and modelling.

Think of MATLAB as a calculator + programming environment + visualization tool.

3

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

4. Why MATLAB for Engineering Students?

• Solve mathematical problems quickly.
• Visualize functions and data instead of only calculating numbers.
• Experiment by changing parameters and immediately seeing the effect.
• Build a foundation for ODEs, PDEs, signal processing, AI/ML and engineering simulation.

MATLAB is especially useful when mathematics and computation need to work together.

4

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

5. MATLAB User Interface

Main areas

Also useful

• Command Window – type and execute commands.
• Workspace – view variables currently in memory.
• Current Folder – manage files and folders.
• Command History – revisit previously executed commands.

• Editor – write and save scripts.
• Figure Window – display plots.
• Toolstrip – access common commands and tools.
• Layout can be customized for your workflow.

5

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

6. Command Window

The Command Window is the quickest place to test MATLAB commands.The prompt >> means MATLAB is ready for input.
Try it:
Calculate 12^2, log(10), cos(pi).

>> 2 + 3
ans =
     5

>> sqrt(25)
ans =
     5

>> sin(pi/2)
ans =
     1

6

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

7. Workspace

What you see

Example

• Variable name
• Value
• Size
• Class / data type

• Enter: x = 25
• MATLAB creates x.
• The Workspace shows x and its value.
• Variables remain available until cleared.

7

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

8. Current Folder

The Current Folder tells MATLAB where files are being stored or searched for.Use pwd to display the current folder and ls to list its contents.
Try it:
Use pwd. Identify your current working folder.

pwd

ls

cd('C:\MATLAB\MyFiles')

8

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

9. Command History & Editor

Command History stores commands you have already executed.The Editor is useful when several commands must be run together as a script.A semicolon suppresses output.
Try it:
Create a script containing three calculations.

a = 10;
b = 20;
c = a + b;

% Save these commands as a script
% Example: first_program.m

9

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

10. Your First MATLAB Program

A simple script can combine commands, variables and formatted output.clc clears the Command Window; clear removes variables from the Workspace.
Try it:
Change the name and marks and run the script.

clc
clear

name = 'MATLAB';
marks = 85;

fprintf('Welcome to %s!\n', name)
fprintf('Marks = %d\n', marks)

10

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

11. Basic Arithmetic Commands

MATLAB follows standard mathematical notation.Use * for multiplication, / for division and ^ for powers.
Try it:
Evaluate 15/4, 3^4 and sqrt(144).

a = 12;
b = 5;

a + b
a - b
a * b
a / b
a^2
sqrt(a)
log(a)
exp(a)

11

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

13. Common Mathematical Functions

MATLAB has many built-in mathematical functions.For trigonometric functions, MATLAB uses radians.
Try it:
Find sin(30°) correctly using pi/6.

sin(pi/2)
cos(0)
tan(pi/4)

sqrt(49)
abs(-12)
log(10)
log10(1000)
exp(1)

13

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

14. Vectors – Row and Column

Vectors store a sequence of values.[ ] creates vectors. The colon operator is a convenient way to generate equally spaced values.
Try it:
Create values from 0 to 20 with a step of 2.

x = [1 2 3 4 5]

y = [1; 2; 3; 4; 5]

x = 0:1:10

t = 0:0.1:1

14

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

15. Matrices – Basic Introduction

MATLAB is built around matrices and arrays.Rows are separated by semicolons; columns by spaces.
Try it:
Create a 3×3 matrix and display its second row.

A = [1 2 3; 4 5 6]

size(A)
A(1,2)
A(:,2)
A(2,:)

15

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

16. Useful MATLAB Commands

These commands help you organize and debug your MATLAB session.
Try it:
Run who and whos after creating three variables.

clc       % clear Command Window
clear     % clear variables
who       % list variables
whos      % detailed variable list
close all % close figures
help plot  % get help

% Comments begin with %

16

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

17. What is Plotting?

Plotting converts numerical values into a visual graph.A basic plot needs x-values and corresponding y-values.The plot command creates a 2D Cartesian graph.
Try it:
Replace sin(x) with cos(x).

x = 0:0.1:2*pi;
y = sin(x);
plot(x,y)

17

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

18. Basic 2D Cartesian Plot

The horizontal axis is x and the vertical axis is y.The smaller the step size, the smoother the displayed curve usually becomes.
Try it:
Plot y = x^2 for -5 ≤ x ≤ 5.

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
y = sin(x);

plot(x,y)
grid on

18

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

19. Title and Axis Labels

Good graphs tell the reader what is being plotted.Always label axes and give the graph a meaningful title.
Try it:
Label a graph of y = x^2 with units if appropriate.

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
y = sin(x);

plot(x,y)
xlabel('x')
ylabel('sin(x)')
title('Sine Curve')
grid on

19

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

20. Grid, Legend & Line Properties

Common plot properties include line color, line width and line style.A legend identifies curves when more than one curve is present.
Try it:
Try '--' for a dashed line.

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
plot(x,sin(x),'b','LineWidth',1.5)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
title('Sine Curve')
legend('sin(x)')

20

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

21. Multiple Curves in One Plot

hold on lets you add another curve to the same axes.hold off returns MATLAB to the normal plotting behavior.
Try it:
Add y = sin(2x) to the same graph.

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
y1 = sin(x);
y2 = cos(x);

plot(x,y1,'LineWidth',1.5)
hold on
plot(x,y2,'LineWidth',1.5)
hold off

grid on
legend('sin(x)','cos(x)')
xlabel('x')
ylabel('Value')
title('Sine and Cosine')

21

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

22. Curve Labelling & Editing

MATLAB Figure tools allow interactive editing.You can inspect and modify plot properties, labels, axes and curves without rewriting everything.
Try it:
Open the Figure window and identify the plot editing tools.

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
y = sin(x);
plot(x,y,'LineWidth',1.5)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
title('Interactive Curve Editing')

% You can also use the Figure
% window tools to edit labels,
% lines and axes.

22

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

23. 2D Polar Plot

Polar coordinates use radius r and angle θ instead of x and y.polarplot(theta,r) is designed for polar graphs.
Try it:
Try r = 2*cos(theta). What shape do you get?

theta = 0:0.01:2*pi;
r = 1 + cos(theta);

polarplot(theta,r)
title('Cardioid')

23

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

24. Cartesian vs Polar Plot

Cartesian

Polar

• Coordinates: (x, y)
• Horizontal and vertical axes
• Use plot(x,y)
• Useful for y = f(x)

• Coordinates: (r, θ)
• Radius and angle
• Use polarplot(θ,r)
• Useful for circular/radial patterns

24

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

25. Introduction to 3D Plotting

A 3D curve uses x, y and z coordinates.plot3 creates a three-dimensional line plot.
Try it:
Rotate the Figure using the interactive 3D controls.

t = 0:0.01:10*pi;
x = cos(t);
y = sin(t);
z = t;

plot3(x,y,z)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
zlabel('z')
title('3D Helix')

25

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

26. 3D Cartesian Curve

Parametric curves define x, y and z using a common parameter t.Changing the equations changes the shape of the curve.
Try it:
Change z = t/3 to z = t/6 and observe the effect.

t = 0:0.02:20;
x = cos(t);
y = sin(t);
z = t/3;

plot3(x,y,z,'LineWidth',1.5)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
zlabel('z')
title('3D Parametric Curve')

26

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

27. 3D Surface Plot

A surface is defined over a grid of X and Y values.meshgrid creates the coordinate grid and surf displays the surface.
Try it:
Try Z = sin(sqrt(X.^2 + Y.^2)).

[X,Y] = meshgrid(-5:0.2:5);
Z = X.^2 + Y.^2;

surf(X,Y,Z)
shading interp
grid on
xlabel('X')
ylabel('Y')
zlabel('Z')
title('Paraboloid Surface')

27

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

28. 3D Polar / Cylindrical Visualization

MATLAB can convert polar/cylindrical coordinates into Cartesian coordinates for 3D visualization.x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ.
Try it:
Change 0.2 to 0.5 and observe the shape.

theta = 0:0.05:2*pi;
r = 1 + 0.2*cos(3*theta);

x = r.*cos(theta);
y = r.*sin(theta);
z = zeros(size(theta));

plot3(x,y,z,'LineWidth',2)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
zlabel('z')
title('Polar Curve in 3D Axes')

28

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

29. Mini Hands-on Exercise

Task A – 2D

Task B – 3D

• Plot y = x² for -5 ≤ x ≤ 5.
• Add title, x-label, y-label and grid.
• Change the line width.
• Add a legend.

• Create a 3D helix.
• Label x, y and z axes.
• Add a title and grid.
• Rotate the graph and observe it from different views.

29

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

30. Summary & Practice Tasks

• MATLAB provides an interactive environment for engineering computation.
• Variables, vectors and matrices form the foundation of MATLAB.
• plot and polarplot create 2D graphs; plot3 and surf create 3D visualizations.
• Use xlabel, ylabel, zlabel, title, legend and grid on to improve graphs.
• Practice by changing parameters and predicting how the graph will change.

Practice: plot y = sin(x), y = cos(x), a polar cardioid, a 3D helix and a 3D surface.

30

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
y = sin(x);

plot(x,y)
xlabel('x')
ylabel('sin(x)')
title('Sine Curve')
grid on

19

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

20. Grid, Legend & Line Properties

Common plot properties include line color, line width and line style.A legend identifies curves when more than one curve is present.
Try it:
Try '--' for a dashed line.

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
plot(x,sin(x),'b','LineWidth',1.5)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
title('Sine Curve')
legend('sin(x)')

20

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

21. Multiple Curves in One Plot

hold on lets you add another curve to the same axes.hold off returns MATLAB to the normal plotting behavior.
Try it:
Add y = sin(2x) to the same graph.

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
y1 = sin(x);
y2 = cos(x);

plot(x,y1,'LineWidth',1.5)
hold on
plot(x,y2,'LineWidth',1.5)
hold off

grid on
legend('sin(x)','cos(x)')
xlabel('x')
ylabel('Value')
title('Sine and Cosine')

21

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

22. Curve Labelling & Editing

MATLAB Figure tools allow interactive editing.You can inspect and modify plot properties, labels, axes and curves without rewriting everything.
Try it:
Open the Figure window and identify the plot editing tools.

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
y = sin(x);
plot(x,y,'LineWidth',1.5)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
title('Interactive Curve Editing')

% You can also use the Figure
% window tools to edit labels,
% lines and axes.

22

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

23. 2D Polar Plot

Polar coordinates use radius r and angle θ instead of x and y.polarplot(theta,r) is designed for polar graphs.
Try it:
Try r = 2*cos(theta). What shape do you get?

theta = 0:0.01:2*pi;
r = 1 + cos(theta);

polarplot(theta,r)
title('Cardioid')

23

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

24. Cartesian vs Polar Plot

Cartesian

Polar

• Coordinates: (x, y)
• Horizontal and vertical axes
• Use plot(x,y)
• Useful for y = f(x)

• Coordinates: (r, θ)
• Radius and angle
• Use polarplot(θ,r)
• Useful for circular/radial patterns

24

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

25. Introduction to 3D Plotting

A 3D curve uses x, y and z coordinates.plot3 creates a three-dimensional line plot.
Try it:
Rotate the Figure using the interactive 3D controls.

t = 0:0.01:10*pi;
x = cos(t);
y = sin(t);
z = t;

plot3(x,y,z)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
zlabel('z')
title('3D Helix')

25

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

26. 3D Cartesian Curve

Parametric curves define x, y and z using a common parameter t.Changing the equations changes the shape of the curve.
Try it:
Change z = t/3 to z = t/6 and observe the effect.

t = 0:0.02:20;
x = cos(t);
y = sin(t);
z = t/3;

plot3(x,y,z,'LineWidth',1.5)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
zlabel('z')
title('3D Parametric Curve')

26

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

27. 3D Surface Plot

A surface is defined over a grid of X and Y values.meshgrid creates the coordinate grid and surf displays the surface.
Try it:
Try Z = sin(sqrt(X.^2 + Y.^2)).

[X,Y] = meshgrid(-5:0.2:5);
Z = X.^2 + Y.^2;

surf(X,Y,Z)
shading interp
grid on
xlabel('X')
ylabel('Y')
zlabel('Z')
title('Paraboloid Surface')

27

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

28. 3D Polar / Cylindrical Visualization

MATLAB can convert polar/cylindrical coordinates into Cartesian coordinates for 3D visualization.x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ.
Try it:
Change 0.2 to 0.5 and observe the shape.

theta = 0:0.05:2*pi;
r = 1 + 0.2*cos(3*theta);

x = r.*cos(theta);
y = r.*sin(theta);
z = zeros(size(theta));

plot3(x,y,z,'LineWidth',2)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
zlabel('z')
title('Polar Curve in 3D Axes')

28

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

29. Mini Hands-on Exercise

Task A – 2D

Task B – 3D

• Plot y = x² for -5 ≤ x ≤ 5.
• Add title, x-label, y-label and grid.
• Change the line width.
• Add a legend.

• Create a 3D helix.
• Label x, y and z axes.
• Add a title and grid.
• Rotate the graph and observe it from different views.

29

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

30. Summary & Practice Tasks

• MATLAB provides an interactive environment for engineering computation.
• Variables, vectors and matrices form the foundation of MATLAB.
• plot and polarplot create 2D graphs; plot3 and surf create 3D visualizations.
• Use xlabel, ylabel, zlabel, title, legend and grid on to improve graphs.
• Practice by changing parameters and predicting how the graph will change.

Practice: plot y = sin(x), y = cos(x), a polar cardioid, a 3D helix and a 3D surface.

30

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

%% Step 1: Define symbolic variables
syms x y a b p q
 
%% Step 2: Define the surface equation
z = (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2;
 
%% Step 3: Compute partial derivatives

eq2 = q == diff(z, y);   % q = dz/dy

b_val = solve(eq2, b);   % Solve for (y-b) from q

  Equilibrium

  When a body is in equilibrium, the resultant of all forces acting on it is zero. Thus, the
  resultant force R and the resultant couple M are both zero, and we have the equilibrium
  equations

  R = ΣF = 0

 M = ΣM = 0

  Free-body diagram  is the most important single step  in the solution  of problems  in

  Equilibrium

  When a body is in equilibrium, the resultant of all forces acting on it is zero. Thus, the
  resultant force R and the resultant couple M are both zero, and we have the equilibrium
  equations

  R = ΣF = 0

 M = ΣM = 0





  Free-body diagram, which is a diagrammatic representation of the isolated system treated
  as a single body.

  Free-body diagram  is the most important single step  in the solution  of problems  in
  mechanics.

  Beams – External Effects
Shear, Bending, and Torsion

 In   addition   to   supporting   tension   or
compression,  a beam  can  resist  shear,
bending, and torsion. These three effects are
 illustrated in Fig. The force V is called the
shear  force,  the  couple M  is  called  the
bending moment, and the couple T is called
a torsional moment.These   effects   represent   the   vector
components of the resultant of the forces
acting on a transverse section of the beam
as shown in the lower part of the figure.

ENGINEERING MECHANICS STATICS
  Beams – External Effects
Shear, Bending, and Torsion

 In   addition   to   supporting   tension   or
compression,  a beam  can  resist  shear,
bending, and torsion. These three effects are
 illustrated in Fig. The force V is called the
shear  force,  the  couple M  is  called  the
bending moment, and the couple T is called
a torsional moment.These   effects   represent   the   vector
components of the resultant of the forces
acting on a transverse section of the beam
as shown in the lower part of the figure.




                        S V Venkatesh - Engineering Mechanics Statics – Unit 3 – Chapter 5 – Distributed Forces

ENGINEERING MECHANICS STATICS

The conventions for positive values of shear V and bending
moment M shown in Fig. are the ones generally used.

Introduction
Computational chemistry is a set of techniques 
for the investigating chemical problems on a 
computer rather than using chemicals.
It uses the results of theoretical chemistry 
incorporated into efficient computer programs 
to calculate the properties of a molecule.
The first theoretical investigation was done by 
Walter Heitler and Fritz London in 1927

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Module I- COMPUTATIONAL CHEMISTRY 
Objective of computational chemistry:
To solve chemistry problems by simulating chemical systems ( molecular, biological, 
materials) to provide reliable, accurate and comprehensive information at an atomic level.
Advantages of computational chemistry:
Calculations are easy to perform than carrying experiments.
Calculations are less costly, whereas experiments are becoming more expensive
Calculations are safe than performing experiments.

Scope of computational modeling:
Molecular Properties:
Computational modeling can be used to accurately predict 
the physical  and chemical properties of molecules, such as
Bond lengths, Bond angles and HOMO/LUMO
Can predict the spectra of UV-Vis, IR and NMR
Thermodynamic and kinetic properties
Electronic structure and mechanical properties

Molecular mechanics programs use equations based on classical physics to 
calculate force fields.
It is based on the model of a molecule as a collection of balls( atoms) held 
together by springs(bonds).
Its too fast like a very large molecules like steroids can be optimized in 
seconds and allows geometry optimization .

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Module I- COMPUTATIONAL CHEMISTRY 
•
Molecular dynamics:
Molecular dynamics is a molecular mechanics program designed to mimic the 
movement of atoms within a molecule. The laws of motion to molecule is the 
base for it.
Molecular dynamics can be carried out on a molecule to generate different 
conformation which on energy minimization.
Staggered vs Eclipsed Conformations of Ethane - Master Organic Chem

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Module I- COMPUTATIONAL CHEMISTRY 
•
Semi empirical methods:
Semi empirical calculations are based on Schrödinger equation.
It represents a middle road  between the mostly qualitative results available 
from molecular mechanics and the high computationally demanding 
quantitative results from Ab initio methods.
Capable of calculating transition states and excited states.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Module I- COMPUTATIONAL CHEMISTRY 
Ab initio calculations:
Ab initio calculations are based on Schrödinger equation and it describes, 
among other things, how the electrons in a molecule behave.
The wave function is a mathematical function that can be used to calculate the 
electrons distribution.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Module I- COMPUTATIONAL CHEMISTRY 
•
Density functional theory
DFT are like Ab initio and semi empirical calculations, based on Schrödinger 
equation.
However, unlike the other two methods, DFT does not calculate a 
conventional wave function , but rather derives the electron distribution 
directly.
Density functional calculations are usually faster than Ab initio, but slower 
than semi empirical method.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Module I- COMPUTATIONAL CHEMISTRY 
Applications of computational chemistry.
•
Electronic structure predictions and energy minimizations.
•
Finding transition structure and reaction paths and molecular docking: protein –
protein, protein – ligand interactions.
•
Thermochemistry : heat of reactions, energy of activation, etc.
•
Calculation of many other molecular, physical and chemical properties.

ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY

understanding of chemical systems and accelerating scientific discovery. 
Its advantages in cost-effectiveness, efficiency, safety, accessibility, 
versatility, and accuracy make it an indispensable tool in modern research and 
development.
Computational chemistry is not a replacement for experimental studies, but 
plays an important role in enabling chemists to design and develop the desired 
chemicals/ products.

Principle Features and Content e)

1. Prevent Waste The primary goal is to synthesize the target product with little to no by-
products or waste. Waste treatment adds to costs.

2. Atom Economy Maximize the incorporation of reactants into the final product. Aim for 100%
atom economy using addition/rearrangement reactions.

3. Safer Synthesis Minimize or avoid hazardous substances in synthesis. Example: Use CO,
instead of toxic phosgene in polyurethane synthesis.

4. Safe Products Products should be effective but with reduced toxicity. Minimize harmful side
effects on users and the environment.

5. Design Benign Chemicals Use safer solvents/reaction conditions. Avoid harmful solvents like chloroform;
prefer water, CO,, ionic liquids, or solvent-free systems.

6. Design for Energy Efficiency Reduce energy intensity by using catalysts (e.g., bio-catalysts) and modern
methods like microwave or ultrasound irradiation.

7. Use of Renewable Feedstock Prefer renewable raw materials like biomass over non-renewable sources
such as coal and petroleum.

8. Reduce Derivatives Avoid unnecessary derivatization steps (e.g., blocking/protecting groups) to
minimize waste and enhance atom efficiency.

9. Catalysis Use catalysts to accelerate reactions, reduce energy use, and achieve high
yields with recyclable, selective reactions.

10. Design for Degradation Products should degrade into harmless substances after use to prevent
environmental accumulation (e.g., pesticides, polymers).

11. Pollution Prevention Employ real-time monitoring and control of processes to prevent hazardous
substances. Recycle unreacted chemicals.

12. Accident Prevention Choose chemicals and processes to minimize risks of accidents like fires,
explosions, and toxic releases. Equip facilities with safety measures.

ii) Plug in hybrid electric vehicles often realize more savings in fuel costs than tradition hybrid electric
vehicles. Justiy the statement. (2 marks)
i)
1) Jet deflector - If there is a sudden decrease in available head, immediate closure of the nozzle is required. However, such
a sudden closure or reduction in flow may damage the pipe line and penstock, etc. due to strong pressure waves
generated in the pipe line. A deflector is used along with the spear to deflect the jet and only a small amount of water jet
strikes the bucket.
2) Draft tube - It is a pipe of gradually increasing cross-sectional area, which converts kinetic energy of water into pressure
energy. A reaction turbine is required to be installed above the tail race level for ease of maintenance (repair) work. Hence,
some head is lost. The draft tube recovers this head. by reducing the pressure head at the outlet to below the atmospheric
level.
ii) Plug in hybrids use an electric motor and battery that can be plugged into the power grid to charge the battery, but also
have the support of an internal combustion engine that may be used to recharge the vehicle's battery and/or to replace the
electric motor when the battery is low. Because Plug in hybrids use electricity from the power grid, they often realize more
savings in fuel costs than tradition hvbrid electric vehicles (HFV).

weak solution of ammonia+water. Since water has the capacity to absorb ammonia vapour, the low pressure ammonia
vapour from the evaporator is dissolved in the weak ammonia solution in the absorber resulting in strong ammonia

Heat exchanger and Generator - The strong ammonia solution is then pumped to a generator through the heat exchanger
at high pressure. While passing through the heat exchanger, the strong ammonia solution is warmed up by the hot weak
ammonia solution flowing from the generator to the absorber. The ammonia solution from the heat exchanger enters the

occurs only during heating, this transformation is called the one-way shape memory effect.

The moulding sand should be sufficiently porous so that the gases are allowed to escape from the mould. This gas
evolution capability of the moulding sand is termed as permeability.
Casting defect caused by less permeability of sand -
Blow holes - These are the spherical, flattened or elongated cavities present inside the casting or on the surface. On the
surface they are called open blows and inside, they are called blow holes. These are caused by the moisture left in the
mould and the core. Because of the heat in the molten metal, the moisture is converted into steam, part of which when
entrapped in the casting ends up as blow hole or ends up as open blow when it reaches the surface.

Pin hole porosity - This is caused by hydrogen in the molten metal. This could have been picked up in the furnace or by the
dissociation of water inside the mould cavity. As the molten metal gets solidified, it loses the temperature which decreases
the solubility of gases and there by expelling the dissolved gases. The hydrogen while leaving the solidifying metal would
cause very small diameter and long pin holes showing the path of escape.

3.c. i) Describe any two functions of the coating in the coated consumable electrode used in electric arc
welding. (2 marks)
ii) Explain the working principle of friction welding with a neat sketch. (4 marks)
i)
1) The coatings give off inert gases such as carbon dioxide under the arc heat, which shields the molten metal pool and
protects it from the atmospheric oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen pick up thus, reducing contamination of the weld metal.
2) The coatings provide flux to the molten metal pool, which mixed with the oxides and other impurities present in the
puddle, forms a slag. The slag being lighter, floats on the top of the puddle and protects it against the surrounding air
during the weld bead solidification. The slag covering also helps the metal to cool slowly preventing the formation of a
brittle weld. When the weld is sufficiently cooled, the slag can be removed exposing the shiny weld underneath.
ii) The heat required for welding in this process is obtained by the friction between the ends of the two parts to be
joined. One of the parts to be joined is rotated at a high speed around 3000 revolutions per minute, and the other part is
axially aligned with the second one and pressed tightly against it, as shown. The friction between the two parts raises the
temperature of both the ends. Then the rotation of the part is stopped abruptly and the pressure on the fixed part is
increased so that the joining takes place. This process is termed Friction Welding (FRW).

ii) Explain the working principle of rivetting with a neat sketch. (3 marks)
i) Pitch - The distance between successive crests/roots of threads is called the pitch of a screw.

Lead - The axial distance a screw will advance when the screw is rotated by 360 degrees is called the lead of the screw.

ii) Riveting is a forging process that may be used to join parts together by way of a metal part called a rivet. First, the two
metal sheets to be joined are held in proper relationship and then the holes are drilled through them. The diameter of the
hole is kept slightly more than the shank diameter of the rivet. The rivet is then passed through the hole in such a way that
the pre - formed head rests against an anvil. Next, the tail is forged to form another head. This is achieved by exerting the
pressure on the die bar that covers the buck - tail. The clearance between the shank and hole is filled in when the rivet is
fully set.
